Published Document: 2026-21600 (91 FR 66638)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule; extension of compliance date.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will extend the compliance date for the regulatory provisions mandating the formal entry of merchandise arriving through the international postal network that is subject to partner government agency requirements, subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the
( printed page 66639)
Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, which were published in the
Federal Register
on June 24, 2026. We believe the public will benefit from more time to prepare for compliance with these changes.
Christopher Mabelitini, Intellectual Property Rights & E-Commerce Division, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 202-325-6915,
ecommerce@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 37801) implementing in CBP regulations an indefinite suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption under 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C) for merchandise arriving through the international postal network.[1]
Further, to accommodate the entry of merchandise formerly eligible for the
de minimis
administrative exemption, the interim final rule established a new informal entry process for merchandise valued at $2,500 or less entering the United States through the mail environment, including shipments that would previously have been eligible for the
de minimis
exemption.[2]
The suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption took effect on June 24, 2026. The remainder of the interim final rule was effective on July 24, 2026.
In the interim final rule, CBP made certain shipments ineligible for the new informal entry process for postal shipments. Merchandise subject to Partner Government Agency (PGA) requirements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, are ineligible for the postal informal entry procedures adopted in the interim final rule.[3]
However, in recognition of the time needed for the public to adjust to this formal entry requirement, CBP delayed the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to October 22, 2026. In consideration of the business process changes necessary to achieve full compliance, CBP provided for a delayed compliance date to allow time for the trade to adjust to the new requirement.
CBP has determined that a further extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network additional time to update their internal systems, develop policies and procedures for submission of relevant data, and to develop the technological infrastructure needed to comply with these requirements. Failure to afford the public extra time to comply with these requirements could lead to disruptions in the flow of important international postal shipments destined to Americans. For this reason, CBP is extending the date for compliance with 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to January 20, 2027.
II. Administrative Procedure Act
The Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 551et seq.,
generally requires agencies to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and provide interested persons the opportunity to submit comments prior to issuing a final rule. The APA provides an exception to advance notice and comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public comment thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). CBP finds that good cause exists to issue this document as a final rule under the APA's good cause exception, because notice and comment are impracticable.
Providing notice and a public comment period on whether the compliance date should be delayed is impracticable because the current compliance date would have passed within the time needed to permit the solicitation of public comments on this rule. Because the public comment period would overtake the current compliance deadline of October 22, 2026, importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network would still be required to come into compliance with 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) by October 22, 2026. Those importers and other parties who need additional time to comply would not be able to benefit from the extended compliance period that this rule provides.
Additionally, this rule does not impose any new substantive regulatory requirements on any person and merely reflects the extension of the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) as set forth in the interim final rule published on June 24, 2026 (91 FR 37801). An extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers and other parties additional time to update internal systems, revise business practices, and develop technological infrastructure needed to comply with CBP's requirements. Providing immediate certainty that this compliance date is extended is therefore needed to ensure that importers and other parties avoid incurring unnecessary costs, burdens, and other challenges associated with meeting the initial compliance date. The delayed compliance date does not change the process that importers and other parties currently use for informal mail entries, as established by the interim final rule
( printed page 66640)
published on June 24, 2026 (91 FR 37801), during this period of delay.
The delayed compliance date also does not impose a burden on importers or other parties who have already come into compliance or had planned to come into compliance by October 22, 2026. Importers or other parties may voluntarily come into compliance at an earlier date if they have the processes already in place. October 19, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”) [1]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,[2]
notice is hereby given that on October 9, 2026, Miami International Securities Exchange LLC (“MIAX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing a proposal to make a few minor, non-substantive edits to Exchange Rule 1703, Consolidated Audit Trail Compliance Rule—Industry Member Data Reporting.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Exchange Rule 1703 to make a few minor, non-substantive edits and clarifying changes to provide accuracy and precision within the rule text.
Specifically, the Exchange proposes to amend Exchange Rules 1703(a)(1) and 1703(a)(2) to modify the references to paragraph (3) to instead refer to paragraph (a)(3). The purpose of the proposed changes is to clarify that such references are to paragraph (a)(3) and are not intended to refer to any other paragraph.
In addition, the Exchange proposes to add a closing parenthesis after the phrase “Industry Member Data” for grammatical correctness and clarity in the rule text of paragraph (a)(2). The purpose of the proposed change is to provide accuracy and precision within the rule text.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed changes are consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act [3]
in general, and further the objectives of Section 6(b)(1) of the Act [4]
in particular, in that they are designed to enforce compliance by the Exchange's Members [5]
and persons associated with its Members, with the provisions of the rules of the Exchange. In particular, the Exchange believes that the proposed changes will provide greater clarity to Members and the public regarding the Exchange's Rulebook by correcting grammatical errors and providing accuracy and
( printed page 66748)
consistency within the Exchange's Rulebook. The proposed changes will also make it easier for Members to interpret the Exchange's Rulebook.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule changes also further the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act. In particular, they are designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, promote just and equitable principles of trade, foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, remove impediments to and perfect the mechanisms of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes the proposed changes would promote just and equitable principles of trade and remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system because the proposed rule changes would provide greater clarity to Members and the public regarding the Exchange's Rulebook by correcting grammatical errors and providing accuracy and consistency within the Exchange's Rulebook. It is in the public interest for the Exchange's Rulebook to be accurate and concise so as to eliminate the potential for confusion.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed changes will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed changes will not impose any burden on intra-market competition as there is no functional change to the Exchange's System [6]
and because the rules of the Exchange apply to all Members equally. The proposed rule changes will have no impact on competition as they are not designed to address any competitive issue but rather are designed to remedy minor, non-substantive issues and provide added clarity to the Exchange's Rulebook. In addition, the Exchange does not believe the proposal will impose any burden on inter-market competition as the proposal does not address any competitive issues and is intended to protect investors by providing further transparency and accuracy regarding the Exchange's Rulebook.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
Written comments were neither solicited nor received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days after the date of the filing, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act [7]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.[8]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. articles.title: 2026 updates in CFIUS and European FDI screening laws and practices | Events | Insights - Squire Patton Boggs
articles.summary: 2026 updates in CFIUS and European FDI screening laws and practices | Events | Insights  Squire Patton Boggs
articles.full_text:
Cross-border deals are increasingly scrutinized by foreign investment review authorities, with ever more attention given to supply chain security by national authorities willing to impose conditions on investments to protect ever-widening views on national security.
Please join foreign investment lawyers Peter C. Alfano III, Tyler Wood and Oliver Geiss in an upcoming webinar to discuss important updates and trends with foreign investment reviews in the US, under the authorities of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), European foreign direct investment (FDI) developments and enforcement focus in key EU member states.
This panel will provide updates on key developments, as well as unique practitioner insights and perspectives on the current environment. The discussion will cover the following areas, followed by a brief Q&A.
- Updates on CFIUS practice and new CFIUS initiatives
- CFIUS enforcement priorities and addressing enforcement risks
- 2026 European FDI developments and updates for M&A practitioners

Published Document: 2026-21624 (91 FR 66679)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that Suncity Metals and Tubes Private Limited (Suncity), the sole producer/exporter subject to this administrative review, made sales of welded stainless pressure pipe (WSPP) from India at less than normal value during the period of review (POR) November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024.
DATES:
Applicable October 22, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John Conniff, AD/CVD Operations, Office III, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-1009.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 6, 2026, Commerce published the
Preliminary Results
for this review in the
Federal Register
and invited interested parties to comment on those results.[1]
On August 19, and October 2, 2026, we extended the deadline for the final results by a combined total of 43
( printed page 66680)
days.[2]
The deadline for these final results is now October 16, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that occurred since the
Preliminary Results, see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[3]
The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Commerce conducted this review in accordance with section 751 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
The merchandise subject to the
Order
is welded stainless pressure pipe from India. For a complete description of the scope,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
Analysis of the Comments Received
All issues raised in the case brief submitted by Suncity are addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum and listed in the appendix of this notice.
Changes Since the Preliminary Results
Based on our analysis of the comments received from Suncity regarding the
Preliminary Results,
we made certain changes to the weighted-average dumping margin calculated for Suncity. For a discussion of these changes,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
Final Results of Review
Commerce determines that the following weighted-average dumping margin exists for the period November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024:
Exporter/producer
Weighted-
average
dumping
margin
(percent)
Suncity Metals and Tubes Private Limited
0.74
Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose the calculations and analysis performed in connection with the final results of this administrative review to interested parties within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the publication date of this notice in accordance with 19 CFR 351.224(b).
Assessment Rate
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), Commerce will determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review. Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), for Suncity, we calculated importer-specific antidumping duty assessment rates by aggregating the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales of each importer and dividing each of these amounts by the total entered value associated with those sales. Where we did not have entered values for all U.S. sales to a particular importer, we calculated an importer-specific, per-unit assessment rate on the basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for the importer's examined sales to the total quantity of those sales.[5]
To determine whether an importer-specific, per-unit assessment rate is
de minimis,
in accordance with 19 CFR 351.106(c)(2), we also calculated an importer-specific
ad valorem
ratio based on estimated entered values. Where either the respondent's weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis
within the meaning of 19 CFR 351.106(c)(1), or an importer specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
we will instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
Commerce's “automatic assessment” will apply to entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by Suncity for which the company did not know that the merchandise it sold to an intermediary (
e.g.,
a reseller, trading company, or exporter) was destined for the United States. In such instances, we will instruct CBP to liquidate such entries at the all-others rate established in the less-than-fair-value investigation if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.[6]
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for the company identified above in the “Final Results of Review” will be equal to the company-specific weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review; (2) for merchandise exported by a company not covered in this administrative review but covered in a completed prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review or completed prior segment of this proceeding but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the company-specific rate established for the most recently-completed segment of this proceeding for the producer of the subject merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers or exporters will continue to be 8.35 percent, the rate established in the investigation of this proceeding.[7]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.

articles.full_text:
From supply chain connectivity and logistics to green capital and AI, HCMC Export 2026 offers solutions to help Vietnamese businesses meet international standards and expand their export markets.
Green exports are becoming a competitive requirement.
On the morning of October 22, 2026, at the WTC EXPO International Exhibition Center in Ho Chi Minh City, the forum "Strengthening Linkages Towards Green Exports" took place within the framework of the HCMC Export 2026 - Vietnam's Outstanding Export Products Fair 2026. The event, organized by the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade in collaboration with WTC Becamex Co., Ltd., brought together representatives from regulatory agencies, international experts, and business leaders.
The forum focused on changes in global trade, trends in supply source diversification, and solutions for market expansion. In the context of increasing environmental standards impacting competitiveness, green transition, access to capital, and the application of technology have become crucial requirements for export businesses.
Speaking at the forum, Mr. Le Van Danh, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade, said that global trade is undergoing major changes. The European Union's (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards pose challenges while simultaneously prompting businesses to review production processes, innovate operations, and move towards sustainable development.
According to Mr. Le Van Danh, to enhance their position in the supply chain, businesses need to strengthen connections with regulatory agencies, associations, manufacturers, and international partners. Key areas to focus on include diversifying supply sources, green finance, cross-border e-commerce, and smart logistics. The Ho Chi Minh City Department of Industry and Trade is committed to supporting and facilitating businesses' green transformation and export expansion.
Restructuring supply chains to seize global opportunities.
Speaking at the forum, Alberto Vettoretti, CEO of Ascentium ASEAN, addressed the trend of supply chain restructuring in the context of a volatile market. Businesses and investors are reconsidering production locations and diversifying supply sources to reduce dependence and risk. The trend of shifting production closer to consumer markets (nearshoring) is also gaining attention.
You may also like
The " China +1" strategy creates opportunities for Vietnam to attract investment, participate more deeply in production networks, and expand exports. However, businesses need to meet requirements regarding quality, schedule, management, and market standards; and proactively learn about free trade agreements and connect with partners to take advantage of these opportunities.
From a logistics and cross-border e-commerce perspective, Scott Humanek, Global Head of Inbound Transportation at Walmart, shared solutions to help sellers access international markets. Walmart established an office in Ho Chi Minh City in 2013, supporting sellers through e-commerce and procurement activities in Vietnam.
According to Scott Humanek, complex supply chains require simple, flexible, and highly reliable processes. Walmart is implementing a logistics solution to support Vietnamese businesses in shipping goods to the US and accessing North American customers. In August 2025, the company announced shipping services in Ho Chi Minh City and Hai Phong . Besides full container load (FCL) shipping, less than container load (LCL) services provide additional options for businesses with different order sizes.
Scott Humanek emphasized that service quality, processing speed, and reliability are key factors in building trust. Businesses need to choose logistics solutions that are suitable for their goods and transportation needs.
Green capital and technology support businesses in expanding their reach.
Besides supply capacity, finance is a crucial factor in the green transformation process. Ms. Ma Thanh Loan, Vice President of HOCA and CEO of Auxesia Holdings, stated that capital channels such as green credit, green bonds, and equity investment can support businesses in innovating production, meeting environmental standards, and enhancing export capabilities.
According to Ms. Ma Thanh Loan, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face difficulties in accessing green capital due to limitations in awareness, data, governance, and conversion costs. To improve access, businesses need to prepare financial documentation, a green transition plan, integrate ESG, and build a roadmap for emission reduction. Data transparency and clearly defining investment needs also facilitate smoother collaboration with financial institutions.
From a technological perspective, Jimmy Nguyen, Director of Strategic Partnerships at Arobid, emphasized the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting businesses in accessing international partners and markets. Businesses need to standardize product profiles, ensure transparency of information, and provide relevant certifications. AI can assist in data processing, networking, and identifying business opportunities. The offline-to-online model also helps expand the partner network through digital platforms.
Notably, the discussion session "How can Vietnamese businesses anticipate the next wave of global procurement?" was moderated by Ms. Huynh Dinh Thai Linh, General Director of WTC Becamex, with the participation of 5 speakers. The discussions focused on buyer requirements, supply chain transparency, green capital, and market access strategies.
You may also like
Within the framework of the forum, WTC Becamex, the Center for Technical Support and Sustainable Development (CSED), the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA), and the Vietnam Exhibition and Advertising Joint Stock Company (VIETFAIR) signed memoranda of cooperation (MOU).
The agreement aims to develop specialized trade fair and exhibition platforms and facilitate business-to-business (B2B) networking. The parties commit to working together to support businesses in enhancing their competitiveness, expanding into international markets, promoting green transformation, and moving towards sustainable development.
Based on the discussions at the forum, businesses need to proactively assess their capabilities, improve processes, and seek suitable partners. The combination of supply chain linkages, green transformation, efficient logistics, finance, and technology will contribute to enhancing competitiveness and expanding markets for Vietnamese goods.

articles.summary: USDA Links Apparel Tariffs to U.S. Cotton Purchases  RFD-TV
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (RFD-TV) — The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is developing a new trade mechanism that would reward selected countries for buying U.S. cotton by offering preferential tariff treatment on apparel made with American cotton and textile inputs.
The Foreign Agricultural Service will assume responsibility for the cotton tariff-rate quota process and plans to launch the new mechanism in 2027. USDA says the program will focus on Bangladesh, Indonesia, Cambodia and Malaysia.
Under the plan, USDA would verify purchases of U.S. cotton by participating countries. In return, qualifying apparel produced with U.S. cotton and textile inputs could receive preferential tariff treatment when entering the United States.
The approach is part of USDA’s Great American Cotton Plan, which is intended to expand trade opportunities and strengthen demand for U.S. cotton. The department has not yet released detailed purchase thresholds or tariff terms.
Final program design will determine how much additional cotton demand is created and whether textile manufacturers in participating countries shift more sourcing toward U.S. fiber.

articles.title: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump's tariffs on Canada - DARPAN Magazine
articles.summary: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump's tariffs on Canada  DARPAN Magazine
articles.full_text:
A U.S. food importer has filed a lawsuit in the United States Court of International Trade challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in the New York-based court, argued Trump's use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in a news release.
Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.
The same statute was used the following month to ban imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.
The White House has said Section 338 empowers the president to impose tariffs when a country puts U.S. exporters at a disadvantage relative to exporters in other countries — even though the law had never been used for that purpose.
U.S. officials have said the latest duties are a response to provincial bans on U.S. liquor, Canada's supply managed dairy system and quotas on certain U.S. vehicles.
Tuesday's lawsuit said the Canadian policies don't justify the sweeping tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.
It notes two of the measures — auto quotas and liquor bans — were actually a response to Trump's own tariff measures. The lawsuit also said Canada's dairy supply management involves policies agreed to under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as CUSMA, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.
A Trump administration official, commenting on background, said the president's actions will be vigorously defended in court. The official added that Tuesday's lawsuit won't deter the president's commitment to levelling the playing field for American workers, farmers and firms.
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said Tuesday that in the Trump administration's view, Canada and the United States are not in a trade war.
"We are negotiating some tariffs," Hoekstra said at a conference in Gatineau, Que.
"From our perspective, we don't view the relationship as ruptured. I know that the Canadians look at it differently."
But the Trump administration's actions are leading to consequences for American businesses.
Thomas Gellert, co-chief executive officer of New Jersey-based Gellert Global Group, said the company has "spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry."
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," Gellert said in the news release.
The company is being hit by the trade war on all sides, the news release said. It pays a 50 per cent tariff on imports of Canadian cheese but is also slammed by Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on American-made cheeses its Canadian division sells in Canada.
The company cites the experience of one of its Canadian cheese suppliers to show how the integrated North American market is being disrupted by the tariff dispute. It gets milk from dairy farmers in Upstate New York, which is processed into brie in Canada, which is then sent back to the United States.
"The tariffs hit American farmers and businesses on both sides of that transaction," the news release said.
The case raises concerns beyond Canada, the news release added. If the duties remain unchecked, any president could use Section 338 to impose tariffs and trade restrictions without meaningful congressional control.
The Liberty Justice Center was previously involved in the legal challenge against Trump's use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act of 1977 for the so-called "Liberation Day" and fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.
In February, America's top court concluded it was not legal for Trump to use the statute, known as IEEPA, because the U.S. Constitution very clearly gives Congress power over taxes and tariffs.
The president replaced those duties with a stopgap tariff statute — which also faced a legal challenge — before putting in place levies of 10 to 12.5 per cent on most nations around the world, citing forced labour in supply chains.
A coalition of U.S. states is challenging the use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to hit the world with the forced-labour duties.
Tuesday's lawsuit argues that Section 338 is defunct and has been superseded by other laws, including Section 301. It also says Trump’s tariffs don't meet various requirements for invoking the law, such as a 30-day waiting period.
"Congress already gave the executive branch a tool for responding to unfair foreign trade practices: Section 301, which requires an investigation, public comment and other safeguards," Liberty Justice Center Senior Counsel Jeffrey M. Schwab said in the news release.
"The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff."
The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund.
Picture Courtesy: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin

articles.title: How Tariffs Affect Amazon and Alibaba: Who Wins? - The Ritz Herald
articles.summary: How Tariffs Affect Amazon and Alibaba: Who Wins?  The Ritz Herald
articles.full_text:
Trade rules create winners and losers, often inside one supply chain. A kitchen appliance sold on Amazon might come from a factory listed on Alibaba.com. If the U.S. adds a duty, the American merchant pays more while the Chinese manufacturer feels pressure to cut the price. Neither platform gets off unchanged.
Three distinctions matter:
- Amazon and third-party sellers carry different obligations for the inventory they import.
- Alibaba’s domestic commerce and overseas units don’t face the same exposure.
- Stock prices can react before a tariff shows up in quarterly earnings.
This analysis from Versus Trade follows those threads through policy changes and market moves. How tariffs affect Amazon and Alibaba depends on where goods travel, who brings them in, and what investors already expect from each company.
The tariff timeline after the court ruling
The Supreme Court tariff ruling on February 20, 2026, removed the legal basis for tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. In Learning Resources v. Trump, the justices decided the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give the president the power to impose tariffs. The reciprocal tariffs and drug-trafficking duties from 2025 fell within that decision.
Older Section 301 tariffs sat on separate legal ground. A new forced-labor action came in July. CBP’s July 23 guidance explained how to apply USTR’s additional duties from July 24, including 12.5% on covered Chinese goods, subject to exclusions. The ruling had not ended import tariffs.
September brought more time
The US-China trade truce got extended through January 10, 2027, according to Reuters’ September 28 report. November 10 had been the earlier cutoff. Each side also proposed around $30 billion in goods that could get lighter tariff treatment. USTR’s September 27 statement framed that as a possible future step, not a cut already in place.
Small parcels remain a separate issue
An October 8 Federal Register notice shows the de minimis exemption is still suspended. Duty-free handling for qualifying low-value shipments did not come back with the court decision. Sellers sending small orders directly to U.S. consumers still face customs paperwork and the usual duties and taxes.
Tariff impact on US vs Chinese stocks
The comparison uses Amazon’s U.S. share price divided by Alibaba’s U.S.-listed ADS price. The direction of that ratio captures the gap:
- A rising ratio means Amazon performed better over the measured period.
- A falling ratio means Alibaba did.
- Both shares can drop while the ratio still climbs.
This ratio is a simple way to track relative performance between the two without owning either stock.
Closing prices around policy events
We pulled AMZN and BABA closing prices from ChartExchange’s daily historical price tables. The table below shows unadjusted U.S. regular-session closing prices in dollars. Ratios come from those close and are rounded to four decimals. They exclude dividends, fees, and currency conversion.
Amazon gained 2.56% on the day of the court decision, while Alibaba moved just 0.12%. On July 24, both fell, but Amazon’s 0.66% drop was smaller than Alibaba’s 1.68% decline. On September 28, Alibaba lost less, and the ratio slipped about 0.52% from September 25.
These are movements around policy events, not estimates of what tariffs alone caused. Earnings expectations, interest rates, AI spending, and company news also influenced prices. The US-China trade war was one force among several.
One instrument for the comparison
Versus Pairs offers AMZNvsBABA as a single CFD that tracks Amazon against Alibaba through their price ratio. You can take a relative performance view without actually owning either stock. The published terms list 1:20 leverage, swap-free treatment, and dividend adjustments. AMZN vs BABA trades on weekdays during the broker’s equity sessions. The live terminal specs set the exact hours and server time.
The product is not available in all regions. The broker excludes residents of the United States, Canada, EU/EEA countries, and the United Kingdom, among other jurisdictions. This is an illustration, not an invitation to trade from a restricted location. Spreads, adjustments, and execution can make a CFD result differ from the closing-price calculation.
Amazon tariffs reach sellers before group earnings
An Amazon seller who imports goods from China can face a higher landed cost before the next quarterly report captures the effect. Landed cost includes the purchase price, freight, applicable import duties, and handling charges. A private label operation may accept lower profit margins or raise prices.
Amazon’s international selling rules say the seller or its provider must act as the importer of record when inventory goes to foreign fulfillment centers. Using FBA does not hand every merchant’s customs bill to Amazon. Tariffs on Amazon listings don’t mean Amazon’s own cost of goods sold goes up by the same amount.
Merchants can pass the pressure along
Many Amazon sellers can absorb an increased cost for a while. When replacement inventory comes in at higher prices, that gets harder. The pressure can move through three stages:
- An importer pays more to restock a product.
- The merchant trims discounts, ad spend, or the next purchase order.
- Customers accept price hikes, switch products, or delay spending.
Amazon might process fewer units or earn less from advertising. Its own imported inventory carries more direct exposure. A U.S.-based seller remains affected by tariffs when the products come from China.
AWS provides an earnings buffer
Amazon data from the June quarter put AWS operating income at $16.6 billion, against $27.5 billion for the group. About 60% came from cloud services. The main profit source sits outside retail.
That buffer isn’t complete. AI infrastructure requires equipment, and softer corporate demand can affect cloud customers. Tariff relief won’t guarantee that the investment produces the returns shareholders expect.
Alibaba tariffs exposure extends beyond U.S. parcels
Alibaba Group runs wholesale trade through Alibaba.com, overseas retail through AliExpress, and domestic commerce through Taobao and Tmall. Lazada adds Southeast Asian exposure, including Indonesia. When someone buys and sells within China, a U.S. duty doesn’t touch that transaction directly.
That distinction matters for ongoing market analysis and trading insights. Alibaba stock can move on export conditions, while domestic competition, consumer spending, and cloud demand pull earnings in other directions. National identity alone tells you little about which operation bears the cost.
The latest accounts separate different pressures
The June-quarter 2026 release merged the former International Digital Commerce Group with China Commerce, Freshippo, and certain Cainiao commerce businesses under the Alibaba E-commerce Group.
It disclosed differing growth rates:
- International E-commerce revenue fell 1% year over year.
- Global wholesale revenue grew 7%.
- AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue rose 45%.
Those figures don’t isolate tariff damage. A Chinese supplier may discount to retain an American buyer while its marketplace still earns service revenue. Lost export orders can also weaken domestic confidence, bringing indirect pressure to operations that never ship to America.
Versus Trade market analyst Amir Razak wrote in his September 24 FXStreet analysis: “Cloud growth, margins, and free cash flow reveal more about the return on each buildout.” That comparison remains relevant when tariff headlines dominate.
Where the higher U.S. border bill lands
The importer makes the initial payment, but suppliers, merchants, and consumers may share the eventual burden.
For many sellers, sourcing strategies become the next pressure point. A new supplier may offer lower labor costs but require different tooling or larger minimum orders. Domestic suppliers can shorten routes while charging more. Domestic manufacturing doesn’t instantly replace the economics of bringing products from China.
Tariff rates are only part of that calculation. Freight, quality control, storage, and customs clearance can offset a cheaper factory quote. Extra inventory protects deliveries but ties up cash, leaving less available for advertising or the next order. A policy pause helps planning without removing those costs.
This analysis of everyday ecommerce operations describes inventory and fulfillment problems beneath a storefront. Tariff disruption adds another moving part: purchase orders, warehouse records, and customer promises have to remain aligned while replenishment economics change.
Indonesia is not a shortcut around origin rules
Importers can’t simply avoid paying applicable duties by routing Chinese goods through Indonesia. Country-of-origin rules depend on production history. A different shipping address doesn’t establish a new origin.
Businesses can diversify legitimately, but moving production takes time and can cause supply chain disruptions. An Indonesian merchant importing for domestic sale faces Indonesia’s rules. One supplying American buyers has to account for U.S. treatment of the goods. The marketplace account’s location doesn’t settle either question.
Risks that can overturn the comparison
Policy can reverse overnight. A pause can become a new escalation, while product exclusions can change the impact on individual sellers. A ratio position remains exposed even when both companies benefit from the same announcement.
Alibaba, China, currency, and company risk
Alibaba carries China-specific regulatory and U.S. listing risks. BABA represents depositary shares, so developments affecting the ADS structure or market access can matter independently of tariffs. That doesn’t establish that delisting is imminent.
Both prices in the table are in dollars, but the businesses earn across currencies. Renminbi movements can affect Alibaba’s translated earnings and investor expectati

articles.title: 'Built on respect': EU gives International Criminal Court its top human rights prize as U.S. sanctions threaten to cut it off - Fortune
articles.summary: 'Built on respect': EU gives International Criminal Court its top human rights prize as U.S. sanctions threaten to cut it off  FortuneUS-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award  Al JazeeraInternational Criminal Court Wins E.U.’s Top Human Rights Prize  The New York TimesTrump-sanctioned ICC wins EU Parliament’s human rights prize  POLITICO.euEU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
The International Criminal Court and its embattled staff have won the European Union’s top human rights honor, the Sakharov Prize, an official said Thursday.
The award came just days after the Trump administration announced sweeping new sanctions on the court, which is based in The Hague, Netherlands, as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said.
Her announcement at the parliament in Strasbourg, France, was greeted with a standing ovation.
The annual EU award, named after Soviet dissident and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov, was created in 1988 to honor individuals or groups who defend human rights and basic freedoms.
A court under fire welcomes the award
ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan welcomed the award, saying that it “comes at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” she said in a statement.
The ICC opened in 2002 as a court of last resort to prosecute senior leaders it deems responsible for crimes that, according to its founding treaty, “deeply shock the conscience of humanity.” It has jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
The Trump administration’s sanctions cut off the court from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and even using U.S. dollars. They set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.
The EU considers options to respond
In a statement after their summit last week, EU leaders said that the 27-nation bloc “deeply regrets” the Trump administration’s sanctions move and “urges the United States to reverse these latest measures.”
They noted that the U.S. has delayed the full impact of the sanctions by six months, and that “this creates space for diplomacy,” and expressed hope that the measures can ultimately be reversed.
Should diplomacy fail, however, the leaders insisted on “the EU’s readiness to take all necessary measures.”
They tasked the European Commission “to take all appropriate initiatives” to help protect the ICC and mitigate the impact of the sanctions, “specifically towards EU companies so that they can continue providing services to the Court.”
One possible retaliatory measure is the EU “blocking statute,” which could be used to protect European court staff, and possibly the Dutch-based court itself, by preventing European companies from complying with the U.S. measures.
An award for when rights and justice come under attack
The ICC and its officials were nominated for the prize by the Socialist and Democrats group in the European Parliament. The group, which unites center-left parties across Europe, said that it was “proud to have put forward their candidacy at a time when international justice is under attack.”
The Sakharov winner is chosen by the European Parliament’s president and top EU lawmakers from among candidates nominated by the parliament’s various political groups. The assembly says the award is “the highest tribute paid by the European Union to human rights work.”
Imprisoned Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu and Taraneh and Romina Rahimi — twins being held in prison for taking part in demonstrations against the Iranian government — were the others to make the EU shortlist.
Last year’s prize went to journalists Andrzej Poczobut and Mzia Amaghlobeli, who were imprisoned in Belarus and Georgia, respectively. Metsola said at the time that “their courage has made them symbols of the struggle for freedom and democracy.”
Several Sakharov laureates, including Nelson Mandela, Malala Yousafzai, Denis Mukwege and Nadia Murad, went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won the Nobel Peace Prize last year, picked up the Sakharov Prize in 2024.
___
Mike Corder reported from The Hague, Netherlands.

articles.title: Opinion: Malaysia's industrial know-how has a world of opportunity - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Opinion: Malaysia's industrial know-how has a world of opportunity  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
Malaysia's export success is well documented. Electronics, palm oil and manufactured goods dominate the discussion. Yet some of our companies have built substantial businesses overseas doing something quite different such as designing water treatment facilities, operating power stations and providing engineering services.
Consider Ranhill Utilities (KL:RANHILL). In Thailand, it operates water, wastewater and reclaimed-water facilities serving industrial estates. In China, it holds a 40% stake in a venture operating 15 industrial wastewater treatment plants with a combined capacity of 267 million litres a day. Its Thai operations add another 119 million litres daily. These overseas operations draw on decades of engineering and operating experience developed in Malaysia.
YTL Power International (KL:YTLPOWR) offers another example. Around 85% of its RM21.8 billion revenue in its 2025 financial year came from overseas operations. Singapore and the UK accounted for a substantial share of overseas operations.
That concentration is interesting. It shows how successful Malaysian companies have become in certain international markets, while suggesting there is room to develop businesses elsewhere.
What interests me is where this experience could take Malaysian companies next. Across Africa and Latin America, investors are putting money into ports, energy, industrial facilities and logistics. Malaysian companies may not be the largest financiers of these projects, but they have spent years learning how to build and operate the infrastructure around them.
According to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Latin America attracted US$188 billion (RM767.4 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025, an increase of 14%. Africa received around US$70 billion, while developing Asia attracted US$644 billion. The figures vary considerably between regions. In Latin America, announced greenfield investment actually fell by roughly a third despite higher overall investment. Yet governments and businesses across these economies continue to invest in industrial infrastructure, energy, logistics and manufacturing, creating potential demand for capabilities Malaysian companies already possess.
Salcon (KL:SALCON), for instance, has undertaken water and wastewater projects across ten Asian countries. Ranhill Worley has worked on Brazil's P-82 offshore production project, demonstrating that Malaysian engineering firms can participate in technically demanding projects well beyond Southeast Asia.
There are different ways to enter these markets. Some companies provide engineering services or equipment. Others invest in facilities, manage concessions or operate plants under long-term agreements. Each approach comes with its own risks, particularly when projects involve long-term financing and operating commitments.
YTL Power owns 45% of the 554-megawatt Attarat power plant in Jordan, which sells electricity to the state utility under a 30-year agreement. The project's development and financing experience illustrates the complexities of investing in large-scale infrastructure overseas, where long-term commitments require careful management of contractual, financial and operating risks. Sapura Energy's experience in Brazil offers another reminder of the financial risks, with the group recording RM2.6 billion in impairments in its 2023 financial year amid restructuring difficulties and cost pressures.
Anyone involved in cross-border business development will recognise the gap between a promising introduction and a bankable project. Finding an interested customer is often the easy part. Establishing who will pay, how the project will be financed and whether the local partner can deliver is where much of the work begins.
Malaysia's trade with Africa reached RM65.11 billion in 2025, including RM34.05 billion in exports. During the first eight months of 2026, exports to the continent amounted to RM21.74 billion, roughly 1.6% of Malaysia's total exports. Africa also received RM7 billion in Malaysian outward direct investment flows in 2025, notably in Mauritius and Angola. Asia still accounted for RM339 billion of Malaysia's RM589.3 billion overseas investment stock.
The figures suggest considerable scope to broaden Malaysia's commercial presence, particularly in utilities, industrial services, food processing and manufacturing.
South America offers a different opportunity. Brazil already has sophisticated manufacturers and engineering firms, so Malaysian companies would need to bring specialist expertise or operational efficiencies. Industrial water reuse, energy efficiency and environmental engineering are areas worth examining. The challenge is identifying specific projects where that expertise can compete.
One development worth watching is the growing presence of Gulf investors across Africa and Latin America. In April, UAE-based DP World launched a logistics corridor connecting Brazil's Port of Santos with Angola and Mozambique, supported by its South African operations. The corridor links terminals, warehouses and freight services, helping Brazilian exporters reach African markets.
That same month, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Capital closed a US$900 million Brazil investment fund. Its wider Brazilian portfolio includes energy and transport infrastructure businesses. These investments are interesting because they create commercial networks around which other businesses can develop.
A Malaysian wastewater specialist could work with a Gulf-backed industrial developer in Africa. An engineering firm might supply services to an infrastructure project in Brazil. A manufacturer could explore local production alongside regional partners. There is an interesting commercial proposition here: Gulf capital, Malaysian industrial expertise and access to African or Latin American markets.
There are no guaranteed contracts in this arrangement. Chinese, Indian, Turkish and Korean contractors are already active in these markets, often supported by financing packages. Malaysian firms would need to compete on their operating experience, technical strengths and ability to deliver. But it offers a route into projects without requiring Malaysian companies to finance every development themselves.
Matrade's Third Country Training Programme (TCTP), now in its tenth year, is one example of Malaysia's longstanding South-South cooperation. In partnership with Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), its latest programme brought together representatives from eight African countries, alongside observers from the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the African Union Development Agency– New Partnership for Africa’s Development (AUDA – NEPAD). The relationships developed through initiatives like these could provide a starting point for identifying actual projects and commercial partners.
The practical work begins with understanding what makes these projects viable. An engineering company considering an African wastewater concession needs to understand the regulator, customer, tariff structure and financing arrangements. A firm pursuing work in Brazil needs access to procurement opportunities and reliable local partners.
These overseas operations draw on decades of engineering and operating experience developed in Malaysia. An engineer, an operator and a financier approaching a project together may have a stronger proposition than a single company working alone.
The UNCTAD World Investment Forum in Doha from Oct 25-27 will bring together governments, investors and development institutions. It will offer another opportunity to see where international capital is heading.
Malaysia already has companies with the technical experience, overseas operating records and knowledge of what can go wrong. What is less developed is a systematic way of connecting them with investors and projects in markets beyond their established territories. That seems a more worthwhile next step than simply adding another destination to our export promotion calendar.
We have become good at making things for the world. Perhaps there is an equally interesting business in helping the world build and run things.
Salim Abu Haniffa is executive director of the Malaysian Chamber of Commerce — Southern Africa.

articles.title: Philippines’ FDI slowdown exposes uneven investment prospects across S-E Asia - The Business Times
articles.summary: Philippines’ FDI slowdown exposes uneven investment prospects across S-E Asia  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Inflows are slipping as regional rivals draw tech projects, putting pressure on Manila
[MANILA] Foreign direct investment (FDI) into the Philippines fell by nearly a quarter in the first seven months of 2026, raising concerns about the country’s ability to attract corporate capital as South-east Asian rivals capture more technology-linked investment.
Net FDI inflows reached nearly US$4.1 billion in the January-to-July period, down 23.9 per cent from almost US$5.4 billion a year earlier, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) data showed.
The central bank has lowered its full-year projection from US$7 billion to US$6.5 billion.
Ser Percival Pena-Reyes, senior research fellow at the Ateneo Center for Economic Research and Development, said that high global borrowing costs, competition from regional rivals, persistent domestic concerns over power costs, infrastructure bottlenecks and a lack of policy clarity are among the possible reasons for the weakness.
Those pressures come as neighbouring economies draw investment into electronics, semiconductors, data centres and artificial intelligence.
The slowdown also coincides with a weaker growth outlook. In its September Asian Development Outlook, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) cut its Philippine growth forecast for 2026 to 3.3 per cent from 3.8 per cent in July.
The Philippines was one of four developing South-east Asian economies to receive a downgrade, alongside Brunei, Cambodia and Myanmar.
Divergence from its neighbours
The contrast with regional investment trends is sharp. While estimates from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development put Asean’s 2025 FDI inflows at US$243.9 billion – up about 10 per cent from US$222.3 billion in 2024 – the capital is not spreading evenly.
In 2025, Singapore attracted US$150.9 billion, while Indonesia received US$21.4 billion and Vietnam US$20.4 billion. Thailand’s inflows rose by about 30 per cent year on year to US$19.1 billion, while Malaysia’s increased by over 50 per cent to US$15.4 billion.
Philippine inflows, meanwhile, fell 4.3 per cent to US$9 billion, exposing how far Manila sits from the region’s principal investment magnets.
Malaysia offers the clearest evidence of the digital-investment boom. It approved RM95.8 billion (US$23.5 billion) of data-centre and cloud-computing investment in the first half of 2026, close to 44 per cent of all approved investment.
Vietnam showed a different but related dynamic: export-oriented manufacturing and electronics supply chains are drawing capital.
At a briefing on Sep 23, James Villafuerte, ADB’s regional lead economist for South-east Asia, said the “top three economies where forecasts have been upgraded” are Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand. “Their upgrades are basically related to technology and export performance as well as strong inflows of FDI.”
ADB projected economic growth of 7.8 per cent for Vietnam and 4.9 per cent for Malaysia, against 4.7 per cent for developing South-east Asia overall.
Villafuerte said that AI and digital technology were a “big upside” for Asean, since the region supplies about a quarter of global semiconductor materials and accounts for about a third of data-centre capacity in the Asia-Pacific.
“Aside from exports, what we are also seeing is that AI and digital technology-related FDI inflow has actually increased. FDI growth in the region is (in the) double (digits),” he said.
He added that much of it in the digital and information and communications technology sectors.
The Philippines’ predicament
For Manila, the challenge is to secure a larger role in an investment cycle that is already concentrating capital and capacity in established technology and electronics hubs.
The Philippines is pursuing opportunities through the Luzon Economic Corridor and the US-led Pax Silica initiative, aimed at securing semiconductor, AI and critical mineral supply chains.
Despite net FDI falling, there have been signs of investor interest. The Philippine Economic Zone Authority has approved 297.1 billion pesos (US$4.6 billion) of ecozone investments between January and September, nearly doubling year on year.
Those approvals are not equivalent to realised FDI, and are yet to translate into sustained capital inflows. BSP figures, however, point to weaker investment momentum, rather than a wholesale foreign capital retreat.
July net inflows fell 44.1 per cent year on year to US$689 million, but increased 54.1 per cent from June to reach the highest monthly level since January.
Monthly FDI flows can be volatile, Pena-Reyes warned. The cumulative decline suggests weakness extending beyond a single month.
Inter-company loans and reinvested earnings are often the most telling signals of how multinational parent companies view their local operations.
BSP data showed that foreign parent firms became more cautious about extending funding to and retaining profits in their Philippine units.
Net investment in debt instruments, consisting mainly of financing between foreign direct investors and their Philippine affiliates, fell 30.6 per cent to US$2.4 billion in January to July. It remained the largest component of FDI and accounted for most of the decline in total inflows.
Reinvested earnings fell 14.2 per cent to US$968 million over the same period, while net equity investment, excluding reinvested earnings, declined 6.9 per cent to US$675 million.
Pena-Reyes cautioned against attributing the decline to a single cause.
Global financing conditions and regional competition sit alongside longstanding domestic concerns, making both the cost of doing business and the predictability of investment conditions important considerations.
He called for more consistent policies, faster project approvals, fewer bureaucratic obstacles and improvements in infrastructure and energy reliability to ensure investment commitments turn into “actual sustained capital inflows”.
Villafuerte said that regional trade integration could help the Philippines diversify towards emerging opportunities and attract more investments.
He pointed to the Philippine government’s trade agenda as a potential offset to the country’s reliance on the US market, where its electronics exports are heavily concentrated and vulnerable to trade diversion.
As at September, he said, the trade ministry had concluded or was actively negotiating free trade agreements with the EU, South Korea, Canada, India, Israel and Chile.

UK Publishes Revised Tariff Preference Utilisation Statistics for 2024
The United Kingdom has released statistics on how far businesses used tariff preferences available to them for imports and exports under preferential trade agreements in 2024, according to the government statistics release. The dataset, issued by the government statistics service, also covers trade in goods between Great Britain and the European Union under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, spanning the period after the UK left the EU.
On 22 October 2026, the export database and aggregate tables were updated to incorporate revised data supplied by non-EU partners, specifically Norway, along with revised EU data drawn from the Eurostat data source. The revisions primarily affect Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark and the Netherlands.
Preference Utilisation Rates measure the degree to which tariff preferences offered through trade agreements are actually used, in goods where preferential tariff rates exist and are lower than the Most Favoured Nation rate. A rate is typically expressed as a percentage and reflects the value of goods traded under tariff preferences as a share of the total value of goods eligible for those preferences, indicating the extent to which a preferential tariff is being applied.
The published materials include several files in OpenDocument format, and the release notes that some of these files may not be suitable for users of assistive technology.

articles.title: The Southern Industry and Trade sector accelerates at the end of the year, contributing to the achievement of double-digit growth targets. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Southern Industry and Trade sector accelerates at the end of the year, contributing to the achievement of double-digit growth targets.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Chinhphu.vn) - In the first nine months of 2026, the industrial production index in the southern region increased by 12.9%, and total retail sales of goods and services increased by 16.5%. To achieve the 2026 targets, the Ministry of Industry and Trade requested localities to accelerate progress in the fourth quarter, remove bottlenecks in investment, energy, exports, and strengthen regional linkages.
On October 22nd, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, in coordination with the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, organized the 12th Conference of Industry and Trade Sectors of Southern Provinces and Cities in 2026.
Attending the conference were Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Phan Thi Thang; Deputy Secretary of the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee Nguyen Sinh Nhat Tan; Standing Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Nguyen Loc Ha; along with representatives from units under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, local Departments of Industry and Trade, and corporations and businesses.
Industrial production and trade maintained their growth momentum.
In 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, amidst global economic fluctuations, tariff policy adjustments, rising input costs, and the demands for green and digital transformation, the Industry and Trade sectors in the southern provinces proactively implemented numerous solutions to support businesses, boost production, and expand markets.
Localities should leverage their strengths in processing and manufacturing industries, high technology, logistics, agricultural and aquatic product exports, renewable energy, and border trade ; while simultaneously strengthening supply chain linkages, connecting supply and demand, promoting trade, and applying digital technology in state management.
According to the report presented at the conference, in the first nine months of 2026, the industrial production index (IIP) for the entire region increased by 12.9%, higher than the national average of 12.3%. Total retail sales of goods and services reached approximately VND 2.86 trillion, an increase of 16.5%, higher than the national average of 13.4%, and accounting for 48.2% of the national market size.
The region's export turnover reached $138.4 billion, an increase of 10.9%, accounting for 31.9% of the country's total export turnover.
You may also like
Industrial, commercial, and energy infrastructure continues to receive investment attention. Many localities are promoting the consumption of agricultural products and OCOP products, supporting businesses in taking advantage of free trade agreements and developing e-commerce.
However, despite the achievements, the industry and trade sector in the region still faces many challenges that need to be addressed. Export growth reached 10.9%, lower than the national average of 24.5%. The progress of power generation projects, industrial park and logistics infrastructure projects has not met expectations; the localization rate and deep processing remain limited.
Strengthening regional linkages and promoting Ho Chi Minh City's leading role.
Speaking at the conference, Standing Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Nguyen Loc Ha stated that Ho Chi Minh City has advantages in consumer markets, trade and services, distribution systems, logistics, and international connectivity. Meanwhile, localities in the region have strengths in industrial production, agriculture , processing, raw materials, and distinctive products.
This creates favorable conditions for localities to build linkages from production and processing to distribution and consumption, improving the operational efficiency of businesses, unleashing the potential of each locality, and contributing to the overall development of the region and the country.
"Ho Chi Minh City has always determined that the city's development must be linked to the overall development of the region and the country. Its leading role is not only reflected in its economic scale, but also in its responsibility to connect, share opportunities, and create conditions for localities to develop together and contribute to common prosperity," Mr. Nguyen Loc Ha emphasized.
At the conference, delegates also proposed initiatives for cooperation, regional linkages, and the organization of industry development spaces in the new phase; and solutions to create momentum for the growth of the Industry and Trade sector in the southern region, making a significant contribution to the double-digit growth targets of provinces and cities in the region.
You may also like
To achieve the targets for 2026 and create momentum for 2027, Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Phan Thi Thang requested localities to focus on managing production and trade in the fourth quarter; remove obstacles and accelerate the progress of industrial and energy projects; ensure energy security and petroleum supply; proactively secure goods and stabilize the market for the 2027 Lunar New Year; and strengthen efforts to combat trade fraud.
At the same time, support businesses in boosting exports, leveraging free trade agreements, and improving product quality; strengthen regional linkages, connect raw material sources with logistics systems and export hubs; promote digital transformation, reform administrative procedures, and improve the efficiency of state management.
Deputy Minister Phan Thi Thang requested that departments and divisions under the Ministry of Industry and Trade closely coordinate with the Departments of Industry and Trade in localities to promptly resolve emerging issues and obstacles. The Departments of Industry and Trade should concretize the conference conclusions into action plans, report to the People's Committees of provinces and cities for guidance and implementation, striving to achieve the targets for 2026 and create a foundation for growth in 2027.

articles.title: Carney says Trump’s tariffs hurt Americans as US Embassy alleges Canadian interference - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.summary: Carney says Trump’s tariffs hurt Americans as US Embassy alleges Canadian interference  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

source_detail.name: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

articles.full_text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised costs for American families and upended decades of trade as he unveiled a $6.2 billion plan to protect Canada’s manufacturing heartland
TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have driven up costs for American families and upended a decades-old trade relationship as he unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan to shield Canada’s manufacturing heartland from the trade war.
Carney also said he spoke with Trump for “quite some time” about issues including trade, as the U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian politicians of seeking to influence American politics ahead of next month’s midterm elections. Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected suggestions of improper interference.
Trump has openly said he wants automakers to move production from Canada to the United States, threatening an industry deeply integrated across the border for decades.
“U.S. tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”
Carney said an integrated North American auto industry would benefit both countries but acknowledged that it may no longer be a priority for Washington. “Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”
Carney said the conversation covered Iran, the Middle East and some trade issues. They discussed Ukraine days earlier. He gave no indication of a breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate.
Trade negotiations collapsed in August after the countries appeared close to a deal. Trump subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.
“It’s clear that Canada’s relationship with the United States has changed permanently,” Ford said. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were.”
Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have fueled a surge in Canadian nationalism. Carney has made reducing Canada’s dependence on the United States a priority, setting a goal of doubling exports to other markets over the next decade.
Carney and Ford announced the 8.7 billion Canadian dollar ($6.2 billion) plan to support steelmakers, automakers and critical mineral development in Ontario, Canada’s manufacturing heartland.
The plan includes CA$5.2 billion ($3.7 billion) over five years for steelmakers and CA$2.5 billion ($1.8 billion) for automakers, including CA$1.5 billion ($1.1 billion) from Ottawa.
The announcement comes as U.S.-owned steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs announced layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, highlighting the toll of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian manufacturing.
Also Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy issued a fact sheet accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to interfere in American elections.
The statement singled out Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for airing a U.S. advertisement featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs. Trump abruptly canceled trade talks with Canada after the ad aired during the World Series in October 2025.
The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections between 2012 and 2026, without linking the cases to Canada’s government.
The administration has launched a whole-of-government effort to investigate and prosecute noncitizen voting, something election experts and administrators characterize as a comparatively small issue. The Department of Justice says that since the start of 2026 it has arrested more than 200 people for illegally voting as noncitizens in past elections, a vanishingly small number compared to the country's tens of millions of regular voters.
“The items featured in the U.S. embassy’s ‘fact sheet’ are not genuine examples of foreign interference and the implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
“Accusing Canada of foreign interference ahead of the midterms could pave the way to ‘Blame Canada’ rhetoric after the electoral results are in.”
Carney said Canada was responding to U.S. tariffs, while Ford denied any interest in interfering in American elections.
Carney said Canadian auto exports to the U.S. have fallen more than 10%, while U.S. exports to Canada have dropped more than 20%.
“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” Carney said.
