articles.title: To improve their position in the supply chain, businesses must master technology. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: To improve their position in the supply chain, businesses must master technology.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The wave of manufacturing relocation and supply chain diversification strategies by multinational corporations is opening up opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in global supply chains. However, attracting large corporations does not automatically mean that domestic businesses become supply partners.
Currently, Vietnamese businesses are involved in the production of many types of components and spare parts, but their presence in high-value supply chains remains limited. Many businesses primarily focus on processing according to blueprints, producing individual parts, or supplying products to higher-level suppliers, rather than working directly with the leading corporations in the supply chain.
Analyzing this issue, Ms. Truong Thi Chi Binh, Vice President of the Vietnam Association of Supporting Industries (VASI), stated: Vietnamese businesses are still lacking and weak, making it difficult for them to participate in the supply chains of FDI (foreign direct investment) enterprises because these corporations usually already have stable supplier networks. Domestic businesses wanting to become alternative suppliers must compete on price and quality.
For large corporations, supplier selection is not simply based on price. Partners must ensure consistent quality across batches, deliver on time, control the process, and maintain supply capacity as orders increase. Changing suppliers also entails evaluation and testing costs and the risk of production disruptions.
Therefore, labor costs or geographical proximity alone are not enough for Vietnamese businesses to win orders. To participate directly, businesses must demonstrate stable production capacity, the ability to meet technical standards, and long-term economic efficiency.
This reality also highlights the need to improve the quality of linkages between FDI and domestic businesses. If foreign investment continues to increase but the domestic supply chain does not improve, the opportunities for technology transfer and increasing domestic value will be difficult to achieve as expected.
You may also like
According to the assessment of the Department of Industry ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), despite achieving positive results, Vietnam's supporting industries still face many limitations, especially in terms of mechanisms, policies, production capacity, and self-sufficiency in supply. The majority of businesses are small in scale, with limited technological and management capabilities, and lack specialized technical support centers, resulting in FDI enterprises' ability to participate in supply chains not being commensurate with their potential.
The core principle is mastering technology.
Experts believe that one of the major bottlenecks is the scale and capacity of investment. To become a supplier for multinational corporations, businesses need to invest in machinery, automation, quality control systems, technical personnel, and production management. Meanwhile, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are limited in terms of long-term capital, technology, and access to market information.
International standards are also becoming increasingly stringent. Besides price and product quality, customers are concerned about traceability, data transparency, environmental standards, and emission reduction. This forces businesses to change everything from production processes to management practices.
According to Xavier Duf, CEO of DXL Research and Consulting, the requirements for suppliers are changing. Besides price and quality, businesses wanting to access the US and European markets need to focus on supply chain transparency, ESG standards, and the ability to provide information about their production processes.
These requirements demonstrate that upgrading capabilities cannot simply stop at expanding production capacity. Businesses need to identify competitive products, invest in the right stages of production, build a quality management system, and develop a technical team capable of improving processes. International certification must also be accompanied by actual operational capabilities, rather than just completing documentation to meet initial requirements.
According to Nguyen Hoang, Chairman of the Hanoi Supporting Industries Business Association (HANSIBA), in addition to the efforts of businesses, the connection mechanism between FDI corporations and domestic suppliers needs to be improved. Domestic businesses need early access to information about component demand, technical standards, order sizes, and supplier development roadmaps. If they only seek partners when their factories are already operating stably, Vietnamese businesses will not have enough time to prepare.
You may also like
In the long term, Vietnamese businesses need to aim for higher-value positions, from manufacturing components according to blueprints to designing, developing products, and mastering technology. With the capacity to research, innovate, and provide technical solutions, businesses will reduce their dependence on outsourcing orders and have the opportunity to participate more deeply in their customers' product development processes.
“The core issue is not just how many large corporations Vietnam attracts, but also what products domestic businesses can supply, at what level, and how much value they can retain. If we don't narrow the gap in technology, quality, and management, Vietnamese businesses risk remaining at the lower levels of the supply chain, even with strong production and export growth,” Mr. Nguyen Hoang emphasized.

articles.summary: ‘Just the beginning’: New Mexico AG warns AI industry after $25B Meta ruling  PoliticoMeta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement  Ars TechnicaHow a Legal Backlash Against Big Tech Is Forcing Big Changes  The New York TimesMeta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case  CNBCMeta has strong chance of getting $25 billion New Mexico penalty slashed on appeal, experts say  Reuters
articles.full_text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the record-setting judgment should encourage more states to take the tech industry to trial.
Fresh off landing a $25 billion judgment against Meta for misleading the public about its privacy protections, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is putting artificial intelligence and Silicon Valley on notice they could be next.
Torrez (D) took a gamble when he opted not to join a $17 billion multistate settlement with Meta in August. But that move paid off with a record-setting ruling against the company Wednesday.
The case relied on consumer protection laws to claim Meta deceived users about its privacy controls, a tactic states are already using against AI developers.
“Anyone in artificial intelligence, people who are building products that they can’t control, people who are making representations in the marketplace about what a product does or doesn’t do, or how it uses or doesn’t use specific types of consumer data, we are going to be watching, and we are prepared to do this again,” Torrez said in an interview. “The message should be received in Silicon Valley that this is not the end, it’s just the beginning.”

articles.title: China’s NDRC issues updated outbound investment rules as overseas investment stock tops $3.4 trillion - Global Times
articles.summary: China’s NDRC issues updated outbound investment rules as overseas investment stock tops $3.4 trillion  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Domestically produced vehicles are ready for export overseas at the Taicang port zone of Suzhou Port, East China's Jiangsu Province on July 14, 2026. Photo: CNS Photo
The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China's top economic planning agency, has announced revised administrative measures for outbound investment, aiming to provide stronger institutional safeguards for its development and security.
Government officials and analysts said that the updated rules, which include articles asking companies to make annual reports on sensitive overseas investment, will better protect the rights and interests of companies making outbound investment and help investors guard against risks as China's overseas investment expands in a more volatile global market.
The rules support investors conducting outbound investment according to market principles and participating in international cooperation and competition. Investors have the right to make their own investment decisions, bear their own risks, and assume responsibility for their own profits and losses, according to a notice posted on the NDRC's website on Thursday.
The new rules requested pre-investment approval by the NDRC for projects in sensitive countries and regions such as those in conflict and sectors such as weapon development and cross-border water resource development. Non-sensitive investment exceeding $300 million needs to go through a file and documentation process.
Along with high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, China's outbound investment has achieved substantial development, with flows rising from $158.3 billion in 2017 to $213.6 billion in 2025, and the overall investment stock increasing from $1.8 trillion to $3.4 trillion. Outbound investment has steadily promoted the "going global" of Chinese products, services, brands, and standards, enabling domestic investors to obtain investment returns and creating many job opportunities, an NDRC official said in a statement posted on the agency's website on Thursday.
However, the external environment has undergone complex and profound changes, with rising unilateralism and protectionism and frequent local conflicts and turbulence, increasing the risks of outbound investment, the NDRC official said, explaining the necessity of the new measures.
In addition, a small number of countries and regions have in recent years adopted discriminatory measures, with some requiring the Chinese side to provide technology or data or to dispose of equity or assets, harming China's rights and interests.
In response to such issues, the new measures implement the provisions on outbound investment protection under the State Council's regulations on outbound investment, improve the reporting system for major adverse situations, and establish an annual reporting system for outbound investment information, the NDRC official said, noting that investors reporting such situations to the administrative authorities will help pool efforts to protect outbound investment rights and interests.
The new rule will take effect on December 1, superseding the incumbent rule imposed in 2017.
Song Wei, a professor at the School of International Relations and Diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told the Global Times on Thursday that the new measure will further Chinese companies' "going global" drive by setting up more safeguard mechanisms to cope with rising risks in overseas markets amid protectionist headwinds, rising unilateralism and geopolitical conflicts.
"The enhanced protection and service by government departments as well as the improved reporting system will enhance companies' ability to avert and overcome risks and market failure, encouraging outbound investment to grow in both scale and quality," the expert said.
At a press conference held by the State Council Information Office on Thursday, an official with China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) noted that that during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, China's two-way investment remained among the world's leaders.
Cumulative utilized foreign direct investment over the five years exceeded $750 billion, and non-financial outbound direct investment covered nearly 190 countries and regions, with cumulative investment exceeding $800 billion over the five years, according to Vice Commerce Minister Jiang Chenghua.
China's outbound investment stock ranked among the world's top three for nine consecutive years as of the end of 2025. In the first three quarters of this year, outbound direct investment reached $128.62 billion, achieving steady and orderly development, according to the MOFCOM.
Analysts said that as China's outbound investment continues to expand in scale and improve in structure, many emerging markets stand to benefit.
"China's robust growth in manufacturing upgrading offers a wide range of opportunities for developing countries in terms of overseas investment and international supply chain cooperation," Wichai Kinchong Choi, a senior expert at Thailand's Kasikorn Bank, told the Global Times on Thursday.
In recent years, China's investment in Thailand has become increasingly technology-intensive, covering fields such as electronic components, circuit boards, smart home appliances, data centers, and electric vehicles. These investments are highly consistent with Thailand's industrial development direction and are areas the Thai government intends to develop, playing a positive role in promoting Thailand's industrial upgrading, Choi said.

articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Global Supply Chain Capacity to Support AI Infrastructure Demand - Konsulteer
articles.summary: NVIDIA Expands Global Supply Chain Capacity to Support AI Infrastructure Demand  Konsulteer
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Substrate agreements with three suppliers target a combined 2.5-fold capacity increase over three years.
- Amkor plans to increase advanced packaging capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028.
- NVIDIA is providing KYEC with a $1.1 billion capacity-reservation advance to support new US testing facilities.
- SPIL aims to increase optical-engine capacity for co-packaged optics by 15 times by mid-2027.
NVIDIA Secures Manufacturing Capacity Across Its Supply Chain
NVIDIA has announced a series of agreements with manufacturing partners to expand global capacity for components used in its AI computing systems, addressing production constraints as demand for accelerated computing infrastructure grows.
Announced at GTC Berlin on October 21, 2026, the agreements involve Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology Corporation.
The collaboration covers semiconductor substrates, advanced packaging, chip testing and optical engines. These components support the production and connectivity of increasingly complex AI accelerators and computing systems.
NVIDIA says the arrangements are intended to increase manufacturing capacity, diversify its supplier base and strengthen supply-chain resilience. Several projects involve new facilities or expanded operations across Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and the United States.
The announced capacity targets remain forward-looking plans, with expansions scheduled to ramp at different points between 2027 and 2028.
Substrate Production Targets 2.5-Fold Growth
NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5 times over the next three years through agreements with IBIDEN, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Unimicron.
Semiconductor package substrates provide the electrical connections between chips and the wider package. Their manufacturing capacity is increasingly important as AI accelerators become more complex and require advanced packaging technologies.
IBIDEN is expanding its Ono Plant in Japan with support from a multibillion-dollar capacity-reservation advance from NVIDIA. The expansion targets production capacity three times its current level at the plant, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in the first quarter of 2028.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics is joining NVIDIA's substrate supply chain, initially contributing capacity from existing South Korean operations. The companies are also supporting facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, with NVIDIA-allocated production expected to represent a significant share of the supplier's annual package-substrate capacity by 2028.
Unimicron is expanding its KF substrate manufacturing operations in Taiwan under a capacity-reservation agreement. The additional capacity is expected to begin coming online in the second quarter of 2027 and reach full capacity by mid-2028.
Advanced Packaging Capacity Expands in South Korea
NVIDIA and Amkor Technology plan to increase advanced packaging capacity in South Korea by more than 300% by the end of 2028.
The expansion includes interposer wafer capacity and new manufacturing facilities intended to support higher production volumes for NVIDIA's current and next-generation computing platforms.
Advanced packaging combines multiple semiconductor components into a package that enables high-performance communication and integration. It is particularly important for AI accelerators that depend on high-bandwidth memory and complex chip configurations.
Expanding packaging capacity can therefore help address a bottleneck beyond the production of the underlying silicon. However, the announced target describes planned capacity growth; actual output will depend on facility readiness, equipment installation and manufacturing ramp-up.
US Facilities to Strengthen Semiconductor Testing
NVIDIA expects its total semiconductor testing capacity to double between calendar years 2026 and 2027, supported by expansion projects in the United States, Taiwan and Singapore.
As part of the plan, NVIDIA is providing KYEC with a $1.1 billion capacity-reservation advance to support new US testing facilities and equipment. High-volume production at the new facilities is targeted for April 2027.
In Singapore, expanded testing operations are expected to begin high-volume production in February 2027.
Semiconductor testing verifies that chips meet required performance and reliability specifications before they enter finished systems. As accelerator volumes rise, sufficient testing capacity becomes an important part of the overall production pipeline.
The planned US facilities also broaden NVIDIA's geographic manufacturing footprint. The announcement does not specify the full locations, final output volumes or the terms governing repayment or use of the capacity-reservation advance.
Optical Engines Become a Priority for AI Networking
NVIDIA and SPIL are also expanding manufacturing capacity in Taiwan for optical engines used in co-packaged optics.
SPIL is targeting a 15-fold increase in optical-engine capacity by mid-2027, with plans to double that capacity again by the end of 2028.
Co-packaged optics brings optical connectivity closer to networking silicon, potentially helping address the bandwidth, power-efficiency and signal-integrity challenges associated with connecting large numbers of accelerators.
As AI systems scale across racks and data centre buildings, network connectivity becomes increasingly important to overall performance. Expanding optical-engine production is intended to support the communications infrastructure required by larger computing deployments.
The capacity targets are ambitious, but the announcement does not provide independently verified production forecasts or quantify the resulting performance improvements for deployed AI systems.
Supply-Chain Resilience Becomes an AI Infrastructure Priority
The agreements illustrate how scaling AI infrastructure requires coordinated investment across multiple manufacturing stages, rather than GPU production alone.
Substrate availability, advanced packaging, testing throughput and optical connectivity can each constrain the rate at which complete systems are delivered. By reserving capacity and supporting manufacturing expansions, NVIDIA is seeking to secure additional production headroom as its AI platform demand grows.
The approach also highlights the geographic complexity of AI hardware manufacturing, with capacity investments spanning several Asian manufacturing centres and new US facilities.
The next milestones will be whether suppliers meet their announced construction and production timelines, and how quickly the additional capacity translates into finished components and deployed systems. For now, NVIDIA's agreements represent a forward-looking effort to address supply-chain constraints across the wider AI infrastructure ecosystem.

articles.title: Built There, Lessons Here: What Pakistan Can Learn From South Africa’s Auto Industry - Pakwheels
articles.summary: Built There, Lessons Here: What Pakistan Can Learn From South Africa’s Auto Industry  Pakwheels
articles.full_text:
South Africa turned a relatively small domestic car market into an automotive manufacturing and export base. Pakistan has factories, international brands, and parts suppliers, but remains heavily dependent on local demand. As Pakistan prepares its Auto Policy 2026–31, South Africa’s achievements and shortcomings offer important lessons.
Pakistan and South Africa have more in common than their automotive industries might suggest. Both have spent decades attracting international manufacturers, developing local assembly operations, and protecting domestic production through government policies. However, their industries have followed different paths.
South Africa has become an established automotive exporter, supplying vehicles and components to international markets. Pakistan, meanwhile, has developed an assembly industry that primarily serves domestic buyers.
In 2025, South Africa manufactured 618,077 vehicles, compared with Pakistan’s 190,082, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers (OICA). South Africa also exported more than 414,000 vehicles during the year.
The difference is not simply a matter of factory numbers. It reflects how each country has developed its suppliers, attracted investment, and connected domestic manufacturing to international demand.
This comparison is particularly relevant now. Pakistan’s proposed Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026–31 introduces mandatory export targets, new localization requirements, and incentives linked to industrial performance.
South Africa has spent three decades experimenting with several of these approaches. Its experience shows what they can achieve, but also where they can fall short.
Pakistan Does Build Cars, but South Africa Builds More
Both countries experienced changes in automotive production between 2022 and 2025. However, South Africa maintained a considerably larger manufacturing base.
| Year | South Africa | Pakistan | 
| 2022 | 555,889 | 235,454 | 
| 2023 | 632,362 | 86,984 | 
| 2024 | 600,171 | 127,702 | 
| 2025 | 618,077 | 190,082 | 
| Change, 2024–25 | +3.0% | +48.8% | 
Source: OICA annual production statistics. Figures include passenger and commercial vehicles, excluding motorcycles. Percentage changes are calculated from the displayed totals.
Vehicle production in Pakistan and South Africa
Annual production, 2022–2025. Units.
Pakistan’s production recovered sharply in 2025, increasing nearly 49% from the previous year. Nevertheless, output remained below its 2022 level.
South Africa’s production was relatively stable across the same period, exceeding 600,000 vehicles in three of the four years.
By 2025, South Africa was building approximately 3.3 vehicles for every one produced in Pakistan.
This does not mean South Africa is immune to economic difficulties. Its automotive industry faces infrastructure constraints, international competition, and changing export demand.
However, it has an advantage Pakistan has yet to develop on a comparable scale: customers beyond its domestic market.
How South Africa Turned Local Assembly Into an Export Industry
South Africa’s automotive transformation did not happen overnight. For much of its history, the country’s manufacturers operated behind import barriers and local-content requirements. These policies encouraged domestic production but also contributed to an industry focused on a relatively small local market.
In 1995, the government introduced the Motor Industry Development Programme (MIDP).
Rather than relying primarily on import protection, the programme encouraged manufacturers to become more competitive internationally. It gradually reduced trade barriers while providing mechanisms that rewarded export activity.
The Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) followed in 2013, placing greater emphasis on production volumes, investment, and local manufacturing.
In his 2009 research paper, Location, Automotive Policy, and Multinational Strategy, University of Cape Town economist Anthony Black explains how South Africa’s automotive industry became increasingly integrated into global production networks after 1995.
However, Black also identifies vulnerabilities associated with the country’s limited domestic market and dependence on multinational manufacturers.
South Africa’s experience demonstrates that industrial protection can provide a starting point. But long-term growth requires manufacturers to develop businesses that compete beyond protected domestic markets.
For Pakistan, this distinction matters.
An assembly plant may supply local dealerships successfully without becoming competitive enough to manufacture vehicles or components for overseas customers.
The Export Difference Is Difficult to Ignore
South Africa’s automotive export performance offers one of the clearest examples of the industry’s international integration.
According to the South African Automotive Business Council, known as naamsa, the country exported a record 414,271 vehicles in 2025.
The combined export value of vehicles and automotive components reached R291 billion, up from R268.8 billion in 2024. Automotive products accounted for approximately 15.6% of the country’s total exports.
South Africa’s automotive export performance, 2025
These figures should not be interpreted as evidence that every South African-made vehicle is exported or that the sector has become fully self-sufficient.
Its export success depends heavily on international manufacturers, established overseas markets, and access to foreign technology.
Nevertheless, overseas demand gives factories opportunities to produce at higher volumes and spread production costs across more vehicles.
Pakistan’s proposed Auto Policy 2026–31 attempts to address the export gap directly.
Under the October 20 draft, passenger car and SUV manufacturers would face mandatory export targets beginning at 5% of factory-gate production value in FY2027–28, rising to 15% by FY2029–30. The policy also proposes financial penalties for failing to meet the targets, alongside incentives for eligible exporters.
The broader ambition is approximately $6 billion in cumulative automotive and parts exports over five years, rather than $6 billion in annual exports.
The important distinction is that South Africa developed export relationships over decades.
Pakistan’s new targets may encourage manufacturers to seek overseas business, but a target cannot independently create foreign customers.
Manufacturers also need competitively priced products, overseas distribution agreements, quality certification, and authorization from their international parent companies.
Why More Exports Do Not Automatically Mean More Local Parts
South Africa’s story also comes with an important warning.
Exporting more completed vehicles does not necessarily mean a country is manufacturing more of their components.
An academic chapter titled Government Policy in Multinational-Dominated Global Value Chains: Structural Transformation within the South African Automotive Industry, published by Oxford University Press, examines precisely this problem.
The research finds that South Africa’s expansion in finished-vehicle exports was not accompanied by a corresponding increase in local content. Much of the industry’s advanced technology and manufacturing capability remained concentrated within multinational companies.
This is an important distinction for Pakistan.
If a vehicle is assembled domestically using mostly imported components, the country still relies heavily on foreign suppliers. Local assembly provides employment and manufacturing activity, but its economic contribution differs from producing engines, electronic systems, and other high-value components domestically.
Pakistan’s latest auto policy recognizes this problem through proposed Minimum Domestic Value Addition Requirements (MDVAR).
For newer manufacturers producing conventional passenger vehicles, the reported requirements would increase from 20% in FY2026–27 to 40% by FY2030–31. Different requirements would apply to new-energy vehicles.
These proposed obligations would link access to concessions with measurable domestic value creation.
However, the real test will be how domestic value addition is calculated, independently verified, and improved.
A higher percentage on paper will achieve little if local suppliers cannot access the equipment, skills, financing, and international orders needed to expand their businesses.
South Africa’s 2035 Plan Looks Beyond Assembly
South Africa is now working under its Automotive Masterplan 2035, which aims to expand manufacturing, increase localization, and create more industrial employment.
The plan includes three notable ambitions: producing around 1.4 million vehicles annually, increasing local content toward 60%, and doubling automotive value-chain employment to approximately 224,000 jobs. These are long-term targets, not achievements already delivered.
South Africa also supports manufacturing investment through programmes such as the Automotive Investment Scheme (AIS), which provides qualifying grants for manufacturers and component suppliers.
This matters because building more local parts requires expensive machinery, tooling, testing equipment, and workers with specialized skills. Pakistan’s new policy takes a somewhat similar direction.
It proposes using proceeds from an Automotive Development Levy (ADL) to support exports, technology upgrades, testing, and vendor development.
However, Pakistan faces an important trade-off. Lower import duties could expose local manufacturers to more competition while localization targets require them to invest in domestic production.
The challenge is to make imported machinery and raw materials more accessible without discouraging investment in parts that Pakistani companies can manufacture competitively. Without a carefully managed transition, competition could lower some vehicle prices while weakening local suppliers.

articles.summary: Global energy power shifts towards Middle East as 72% of industry leaders predict bigger role  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
ADIPEC report reveals how geopolitical tensions, investment and AI are reshaping energy
The year 2026 marks a historic turning point for the global energy ecosystem. Following one of the most severe geopolitical stress tests in fifty years—including severe disruptions in key transit corridors like the Strait of Hormuz, which at its peak removed roughly 14% of global oil and gas supply—the global energy system has demonstrated remarkable resilience.
Rather than collapsing under shock, 64% of global energy insiders state that the system proved more resilient than expected. This adaptability stems not from chance, but from proactive structural shifts: rapid trade re-routing, digital integration, market diversification, and deep strategic realignment.
Three defining dynamics dominate the 2026 outlook:
The Eastward Migration of Influence: The global center of gravity for energy demand, investment, and strategic decision-making has moved decisively toward the Middle East and Asia.
Re-Defining Energy Security as Diversification: Energy independence through isolation is obsolete; modern energy security requires an "all-of-the-above" multi-source strategy.
The Artificial Intelligence Demand Surge: AI is acting as both a technology enabler and a major new energy consumer, driving electricity demand forecasts significantly higher.
1. Geopolitical Realities & The Energy Trilemma
While 77% of executives remain optimistic and 85% highlight increased investment attractiveness, the sector operates under severe strain.
The Security Imperative: Conflict and war rank as the primary sector threat for 42% of general energy decision-makers and 55% of oil and gas specialists. Tariffs/supply chain friction (24-31%) and climate disruption (25-26%) follow.
Diversification vs. Self-Reliance: Only 20% of leaders rank domestic self-reliance among their top priorities for energy security. Instead, security is defined by expanding supply options, building redundant routes, protecting critical infrastructure (34%), and investing in renewables (37%) and gas.
Energy Source Trajectory: Over the next decade, net expectations show increased importance across nearly every source: Renewables (83% net), Natural Gas/LNG (72% net), Nuclear (69% net), and Oil (62% net). Coal remains globally divided (25% net), showing positive expansion outlooks in Asia/Middle East but negative trajectory in Europe (-3%).
2. The Gulf-Asia Corridor: Global Energy's New Center of Gravity
Energy trade, capital deployment, and demand growth have re-anchored along the Gulf-Asia Corridor.
Regional Dominance: The Middle East was selected as the #1 regional opportunity overall (30%) and ranked second in every other region worldwide. 72% of respondents expect the region's global importance to rise significantly over the next decade.
Supplier-Customer Alignment: 49% of oil and gas producers cite Asia Pacific as their primary customer market, closely matched by the Middle East (48%). Conversely, consumers identify the Middle East and Asia Pacific as their primary critical suppliers.
The Asian Divide:
Growth Asia (India & Indonesia): Boasting extreme optimism (86% and 94% respectively), focused on expanding infrastructure and generating rapid baseline capacity.
Import-Dependent Asia (Japan & South Korea): Exhibiting high caution (Japan optimism sits at 23%), heavily prioritizing route protection, reserves, and supply security.
Nuclear Convergence: Nuclear energy emerges as the unifying baseline technology across Asia, supported by 84% in India, 77% in Indonesia and South Korea, and 63% in Japan.
3. Artificial Intelligence: Re-Drawing Power Balances and Demand
Artificial Intelligence is fundamentally altering both operational efficiencies and baseline power infrastructure.
Power Shift to Tech: 43% of energy executives believe Technology and AI firms will hold more influence over the energy industry than governments (15%), financial institutions (15%), or traditional energy giants (14-9%).
Demand Reality Check: 81% expect AI-driven electricity demand to surge past official forecasts (32% expecting demand to be "much higher"). Global data center power consumption is projected by the IEA to reach 950 TWh by 2030.
Pragmatic Adoption Barriers: While 71% see AI as a net opportunity, industry practitioners highlight significant operational bottlenecks:
Legacy System Integration: 83% of AI-focused oil/gas leaders cite difficulties interfacing with legacy infrastructure.
Data Plumbing: Unstructured, non-standardized data across decades-old assets presents the largest adoption hurdle (21% open-text responses).
Near-Term Overestimation: 57% of AI optimists acknowledge that short-term demand impact is currently hype-driven, despite vast long-term structural impact.
4. Capital, Infrastructure, and Execution Constraints
Despite a record $3.4 trillion in annual global energy investments ($2.2T clean/grid, $1.2T oil/gas/coal), capital allocation faces a race against time.
Execution Speed Over Capital Availability: The primary industry barrier is no longer raising capital, but deploying infrastructure at a speed that matches demand.
Energy Insiders: Highlight Renewable Generation (34%), Energy Storage (31%), Grids & Transmission (24%), and Nuclear (24%) as severely underfunded.
Oil & Gas Insiders: Point to Carbon Capture / Low-Carbon Fuels (38%) and Grids & Transmission (35%) as their top investment deficits.
Decarbonization Through Integration: Decarbonization has shifted from a philosophy of asset retirement to one of operational integration. 46% of oil and gas leaders rank low-carbon fuel/hydrogen innovation as the top deliverable to meet future demand, while 38% focus on lowering baseline extraction emissions.
The findings of the ADIPEC Global Energy Report 2026 confirm that the energy transition is not a simple linear trade-off between fossil fuels and renewables. It is a complex expansion of a multi-source, digital-first, globalized energy system.
Having survived severe geopolitical stress tests, the industry has proven its resilience. As capital, technology, and geopolitical weight consolidate along the Gulf-Asia axis, the sector's central challenge over the coming decade is no longer formulating ambition, but executing delivery.
Key statistics
64% say the global energy system proved more resilient than expected.
72% expect the Middle East to become more important in global energy over the next decade.
85% say energy is a more attractive sector for investment than five years ago.
93% say meeting future energy demand will require growth across multiple energy sources
rather than one dominant source.
77% are optimistic about the decade ahead
*. (Source: ADIPEC Global Energy Trends 2026)

articles.full_text:
Capchem
Leading LiFSI capacity and market share
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Lithium Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global Lithium Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) market is undergoing a structural transformation, moving from a niche electrolyte additive to a core conductive salt in advanced lithium-ion battery systems. This shift is anchored in the automotive industry's relentless pursuit of higher energy density, faster charging rates, and improved performance across wide temperature ranges. As electric vehicle platforms evolve, LiFSI adoption is increasingly programmatic, embedded within multi-year validation cycles that prioritize safety, longevity, and reliability.
The supply side is equally dynamic, characterized by complex multi-step synthesis, stringent purity requirements, and significant scale-up barriers. Geographically, demand is concentrating around battery gigafactory clusters in Asia-Pacific, with North America and Europe accelerating local production to meet regional content and sustainability mandates. The forecast period 2026-2035 anticipates robust volume growth, supported by the proliferation of high-voltage battery systems, solid-state battery development, and energy storage applications. However, pricing pressure for high-volume OEM programs and precursor availability constraints will shape competitive dynamics.
This report provides a data-driven view of market size, segmentation, supply chain structure, and key trends, offering stakeholders a transparent analytical framework to navigate the evolving LiFSI landscape.
The baseline scenario for the Lithium Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) market from 2026 to 2035 envisions a period of accelerated adoption, transitioning from a specialty additive to a mainstream electrolyte component. The primary growth engine is the global automotive industry's shift toward electric vehicles, particularly those requiring high-energy-density cells, fast-charging capabilities, and enhanced thermal stability. As OEMs lock in battery chemistries for next-generation platforms, LiFSI content per cell is expected to rise, supported by its superior ionic conductivity and stability compared to conventional salts like LiPF6.
The market is projected to grow at a strong CAGR, with volume demand expanding across Asia-Pacific, North America, and Europe. Supply-side dynamics will be critical; manufacturers are investing in capacity expansions and process optimization to overcome synthesis complexity and purity challenges. Pricing is expected to bifurcate, with high-volume automotive contracts facing downward pressure while specialty applications retain premium pricing. The market index, set at 100 in 2025, is forecast to reach significantly higher levels by 2035, reflecting both volume growth and value expansion.
Key risks include slower-than-expected EV adoption, raw material price volatility, and technical hurdles in solid-state battery commercialization. Nevertheless, the long-term trajectory remains positive, underpinned by regulatory push for decarbonization and continuous battery performance improvements.
Electric vehicle batteries represent the dominant end-use for LiFSI, accounting for the majority of global demand. The mechanism is straightforward: LiFSI enhances ionic conductivity and thermal stability in electrolytes, enabling higher nickel-content cathodes and silicon-dominant anodes that push energy density boundaries. As automakers transition to 800-volt architectures for fast charging, LiFSI's wide electrochemical window and low resistance become critical. Demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, battery pack energy density targets, and charging rate specifications.
Through 2035, as EV adoption accelerates globally, LiFSI content per vehicle is expected to rise, supported by platform designs that prioritize range and charging speed. The trend is reinforced by regulatory mandates phasing out internal combustion engines in key markets. Major battery cell manufacturers and automotive OEMs are locking in LiFSI supply through multi-year contracts, creating sticky demand. However, cost pressures in mass-market EV segments may slow premium LiFSI adoption in lower-tier vehicles, balancing growth across price segments. Current trend: Rapid adoption driven by high-energy-density and fast-charging requirements.
Major trends: Shift to high-nickel cathode chemistries requiring stable electrolytes, Proliferation of 800V fast-charging platforms, Silicon anode commercialization increasing electrolyte additive demand, and Regionalization of battery supply chains driving local LiFSI production.
Representative participants: Tesla, BYD, CATL, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, and Samsung SDI.
Energy storage systems are a fast-growing segment for LiFSI, driven by the global push for renewable energy integration and grid resilience. LiFSI's contribution is primarily in enhancing cycle life and thermal stability of large-format lithium-ion cells used in stationary storage. The mechanism involves reducing electrolyte degradation over thousands of charge-discharge cycles, which is critical for ESS applications where longevity directly impacts levelized cost of storage. Demand-side indicators include renewable capacity additions, government auctions for storage, and utility-scale project pipelines.
Through 2035, as solar and wind penetration increases, ESS deployments are expected to surge, particularly in regions with ambitious decarbonization targets. LiFSI adoption in ESS is supported by its ability to operate across wide temperature ranges, reducing cooling requirements and system costs. However, price sensitivity in utility-scale projects may favor conventional salts unless LiFSI prices decline, creating a balance between performance gains and cost considerations. Current trend: Steady growth supported by renewable energy integration and grid stability needs.
Major trends: Rapid growth in utility-scale battery storage installations, Increasing focus on long-duration storage solutions, Declining battery costs enabling broader ESS deployment, and Policy incentives for grid-scale storage in major markets.
Representative participants: Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, Fluence, Tesla, and BYD.
Solid-state and lithium metal batteries represent a frontier application for LiFSI, with commercialization timelines stretching toward the late 2020s and beyond. LiFSI serves as a key electrolyte salt in solid polymer and hybrid solid-state systems, where its high oxidative stability and compatibility with lithium metal anodes are essential. The mechanism involves forming stable interfaces that suppress dendrite growth and improve cycle life. Demand-side indicators include R&D investment, pilot production lines, and automotive OEM announcements regarding solid-state vehicle platforms.
Through 2035, as solid-state technology matures from lab to fab, LiFSI demand from this segment is expected to grow from a small base, potentially becoming a significant volume driver in the latter part of the forecast period. However, technical hurdles, manufacturing scalability, and cost challenges may delay widespread adoption, making this segment's growth trajectory uncertain but strategically important for long-term market positioning. Current trend: Emerging high-potential segment with commercialization expected post-2027.
Major trends: Intensive R&D and pilot-scale production of solid-state cells, Automotive OEM partnerships with solid-state battery developers, Advances in sulfide and polymer electrolyte systems, and Government funding for next-generation battery research.
Representative participants: QuantumScape, Solid Power, Toyota, Panasonic, and Samsung SDI.
Supercapacitors utilize LiFSI as an electrolyte salt in applications requiring high power density and rapid charge-discharge cycles, such as regenerative braking, grid frequency regulation, and automotive start-stop systems. The mechanism relies on LiFSI's high ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability, which enable efficient ion transport at high rates. Demand-side indicators include supercapacitor production volumes, adoption in hybrid vehicles, and deployment in industrial backup power. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow modestly, supported by niche applications where supercapacitors outperform batteries in cycle life and power delivery.
However, the relatively small market size and competition from alternative electrolyte salts limit LiFSI's share. Growth opportunities exist in emerging applications like wearable electronics and IoT devices, where miniaturized supercapacitors require high-performance electrolytes. Overall, this segment remains a stable but limited contributor to total LiFSI demand. Current trend: Niche but stable demand from high-power applications.
Major trends: Adoption in automotive regenerative braking systems, Use in grid frequency regulation and power quality applications, Miniaturization for consumer electronics and wearables, and Development of hybrid supercapacitor-battery systems.
Representative participants: Maxwell Technologies, Panasonic, Nippon Chemi-Con, and Skeleton Technologies.
High-voltage battery systems, typically operating at 800 volts and above, are a specialized but growing end-use for LiFSI. These systems demand electrolytes with exceptional oxidative stability and low resistance to handle higher potentials without degradation. LiFSI's wide electrochemical window and thermal stability make it a preferred salt for such applications, enabling faster charging and improved efficiency. Demand-side indicators include the number of high-voltage EV models launched, charging infrastructure build-out, and performance requirements for premium and performance vehicles.

articles.full_text:
Given the complex fluctuations in the global market, proactively diversifying export markets while increasing added value is identified as a strategy for Vietnam's wood and furniture industry to maintain its growth momentum and move towards sustainable development in the new phase.
Against the backdrop of a global economy fraught with complex fluctuations stemming from geopolitical factors, supply chain disruptions, and the rise of trade protectionist barriers, Vietnam's wood processing and export industry and wood products are facing both significant opportunities and intertwined challenges.
At the Trade Promotion Conference with the system of Vietnamese Trade Offices abroad in October 2026, organized by the Trade Promotion Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ) with the theme "Diversifying markets, promoting the export of Vietnamese wood and furniture products," representatives of state management agencies, the system of Vietnamese trade offices abroad, associations, and businesses focused on discussing and seeking solutions to expand markets and increase value for the wood export industry in the new phase.
The landscape of the timber export industry: Growth in scale intertwined with barriers from market structure.
According to data shared at the conference, in 2025, Vietnam's exports of wood and wood products are expected to reach approximately US$17.2 billion, continuing to hold its position among the country's top export sectors. In the first nine months of 2026, the export value of this product group is estimated to reach nearly US$13.43 billion, a growth of nearly 6.3% compared to the same period in 2025.
Commenting on these results, Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department, said that this is a noteworthy sign reflecting the efforts to maintain production, seek orders, and the flexible adaptability of the business community. However, the growth momentum also highlights the urgent need to enhance resilience against market fluctuations. Currently, trade policies, tariffs, and trade defense measures in major markets remain key issues that need close monitoring.
Mr. Le Hoang Tai emphasized: “Managing origin, ensuring the source of raw materials, and meeting the stringent requirements of each market need to be proactively prepared by businesses right from the production stage. Therefore, diversifying markets is not simply a solution to find more orders, but must also be linked to enhancing product value and competitiveness. Besides consolidating traditional markets, businesses need to actively explore potential markets and choose segments that match their actual capabilities.”
This orientation is entirely consistent with the "Go Global" program for the period 2026-2030, approved by the Prime Minister in Decision No. 626 dated April 6, 2026, as well as the implementation action plan of the Ministry of Industry and Trade. Market diversification is not simply about bringing existing products to a new location. The crucial element is to clearly understand customer needs, the standards and requirements that the product must meet, and effective channels for reaching those customers.
Alongside improving production capacity, businesses need to pay special attention to product design, development, and brand building, thereby gradually enhancing their ability to participate in value-added stages of the global supply chain.
Providing further information on the market, Mr. Phung Quoc Man - Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Handicraft and Wood Processing Association (HAWA) said that Vietnam currently ranks second in the world in furniture exports, after China , and Vietnamese wood products are present in 167 countries and territories.
This position is built on production capacity, skilled craftsmanship, and the ability to meet the stringent requirements of international customers. Specifically, Vietnamese businesses have the capacity to supply a diverse range of products, from home, office, and outdoor furniture to products for construction projects and hotels. Alongside this, companies in the industry are actively investing in design, technology, management, and the development of legally sourced and sustainable raw materials.
However, a report from the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association (VIFOREST) also points out that the current export structure is imbalanced, with the OEM processing model still accounting for a high percentage and the US market accounting for 55% of total export turnover in 2025 with $9.46 billion, followed by Japan with $2.15 billion (12.5%), China with $2.09 billion (12.1%), South Korea with $0.71 billion (4.1%) and the EU with $0.66 billion (3.8%).
Simultaneously, the current structure of export product groups shows that indoor and outdoor furniture accounts for 65% to 70%, wood chips 15%, wood pellets 7%, wood panels 5%, and other groups 3% to 5%. Although the wood industry's trade surplus reached a high level with an export surplus of approximately US$14 billion in 2025 (exports US$17.204 billion and imports US$3.22 billion), the value added retained domestically remains limited due to increasing raw material costs, logistics, and compliance costs.
Furthermore, the timber industry is also significantly impacted by international legal barriers such as the European Union's Forest Protection Regulation (EUDR), effective from December 30, 2026, for large and medium-sized enterprises; regulations on legally sourced timber (VPA/FLEGT), CITES, FSC, PEFC, and VFCS forest certifications; and stringent tariff policies from the US market, including Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs, as well as anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations on plywood.
These factors are clearly reflected in the actual results: in the first nine months of 2026, the export value of deeply processed wood products reached US$8.56 billion and showed almost no growth due to market fluctuations. Meanwhile, the overall growth of the entire industry mainly relied on wood chips and industrial boards.
Assessing this situation, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai - Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association (VIFOREST) - noted that behind the export figures, there remains a big question: how much value do Vietnamese businesses actually hold, from design and branding to distribution channels? The VIFORES representative also warned that an increase in pure export value does not necessarily mean an increase in the value of deeply processed products.
Potential and opportunities in key markets from the perspective of Vietnamese trade offices abroad.
At the briefing conference, representatives from Vietnamese trade offices abroad provided comprehensive insights into the scale, development potential, and new technical standards that domestic businesses need to be aware of when exporting wood and wood products.
Regarding the Dutch market, Ms. Vo Thi Ngoc Diep, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in the Netherlands, stated that in the first nine months of 2026, total bilateral trade between Vietnam and the Netherlands reached over US$13 billion, an increase of 26.7% compared to the same period in 2025. Of this, Vietnam's exports to the Netherlands reached over US$12.3 billion, an increase of 27.6%.
Notably, wood and wood products ranked second in terms of export growth to this market, with an 86% increase, reaching a value of US$158 million. The Netherlands currently plays a crucial role as a gateway for Vietnamese goods to access importers and retailers throughout the European Union (EU) thanks to its developed port system and distribution network.
You may also like
Regarding consumer demand, Ms. Vo Thi Ngoc Diep stated that Dutch consumers prioritize furniture products with simple designs, multi-functionality, space-saving features, legal origin, and high recyclability. Product categories with significant potential include living room, bedroom, and dining room furniture, outdoor tables and chairs, assembled wooden furniture, and furniture combining wood and rattan.
Regarding the Spanish market, Mr. Luu Van Khang, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in Spain, stated that Spain's imports of wood and wood products from Vietnam have seen a strong increase. According to DataComex data, in the first seven months of 2024, Spain imported approximately US$1.8 million from Vietnam; this figure increased to US$3.94 million in the same period of 2025, and reached US$9.38 million in the first seven months of 2026, representing a 138% increase compared to 2025 and five times higher than in 2024.
Spain has a great need for diversification of supply sources beyond traditional markets. Besides home and outdoor furniture lines incorporating natural materials, the furniture segment for hotel, restaurant, and commercial projects is opening up significant opportunities for manufacturers with flexible design and supply capabilities.
In the Oceania region, Ms. Tran Thi Thanh My, Deputy Consul General of Vietnam in Sydney and Head of the Vietnamese Trade Office in Australia, noted that the timber market in Australia is on the path to recovery, linked to the development of the construction industry and housing demand.
In the 2024-2025 financial year, the total value of Australia's imports of forest products and timber reached approximately AUD 6.83 billion (equivalent to USD 4.5 billion), a 5% increase compared to the previous period. Vietnam ranked 7th in supplying timber to this market with a value of USD 125 million. In the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's exports of timber and wood products to Australia reached USD 125.4 million, an increase of over 7% compared to the same period.
Forecasts indicate that demand for timber in the Australian construction sector could increase by up to 50% between now and 2050. Major potential segments include furniture (HS codes 9401 and 9403), smart and multi-functional furniture, and industrial furniture for both residential and commercial projects. Australian

articles.title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms - CNBC
articles.summary: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms  CNBCUS pulls personnel from Saudi Arabia as kingdom comes under Houthi fire  Fox NewsU.S. troops and diplomats evacuating Middle East posts, sources say  NBC NewsWashington orders US embassy staff, families to leave Saudi Arabia  YahooEXCLUSIVE: US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes  Reuters
articles.full_text:
The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.
The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.
A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.
In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes.
The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year.
Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program.
Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler.
As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.
"China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.
China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.
Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

articles.title: When will the Vietnamese timber industry escape the fate of "wearing silk robes in the dark"? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: When will the Vietnamese timber industry escape the fate of "wearing silk robes in the dark"?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| The over-reliance on the OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) model is putting Vietnam's wood industry under urgent pressure to change (Photo: CP). | 
 Risk pressures from a single market and low-value outsourcing model.
 According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade , exports of wood and wood products are projected to reach approximately US$17.2 billion in 2025, resulting in a trade surplus of over US$13.6 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, export turnover is estimated at US$13.43 billion, a 7.3% increase compared to the same period. This result strengthens Vietnam's position as the world's fifth largest exporter of forestry products and the second largest globally for deeply processed wood products such as indoor and outdoor furniture. Vietnamese wood products are currently present in 167 countries and territories, affirming Vietnam's superior craftsmanship and increasingly sophisticated production scale.
 Commenting on this picture, Mr. Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Trade Promotion Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), stated that the 7.3% growth in the past nine months is a testament to the significant efforts of the business community in flexibly seeking orders and maintaining production pace. However, Mr. Le Hoang Tai emphasized that the volatile international context requires the wood industry to improve its resilience and risk management capabilities. Market diversification is not simply about bringing existing products to new locations, but must be linked to increasing added value, meeting stringent technical standards, and participating more deeply in the global value chain, in line with Decision 626/QD-TTg dated January 6, 2026, approving the Go Global Program for the period 2026-2030.
 Analyzing the internal bottlenecks in more detail, Mr. Ngo Si Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association (VFOREST), warned that the growth of the wood industry still contains elements of unsustainability. The biggest weakness is the risk of market concentration, with the US market alone accounting for over 50% of the industry's total export turnover, equivalent to about $9.5 billion out of the US's total annual wood product imports of $22 to $24 billion. In the context of the US continuously increasing trade protection measures, tariffs under Section 301, Section 232, and the risk of tax evasion investigations, heavy reliance on a single market makes businesses very vulnerable to policy changes.
 In particular, Mr. Hoai emphasized that although Vietnam has approximately 6,000 wood industry enterprises, with over 3,500 exporting companies, and the trade turnover between FDI and purely Vietnamese enterprises remains balanced at 50-50, most domestic enterprises are still struggling with the OEM (Original Design Manufacturer) model. Production based on existing designs and orders results in very low retained value. Despite being self-sufficient in domestic plantation timber with over 3 million hectares of acacia and nearly 1 million hectares of rubber, and controlling $3.25 billion worth of imported timber under the VPA/FLEGT Agreement, the lack of self-designed ODM (Original Design Manufacturer) products and the absence of independent brands mean that Vietnamese products remain at a disadvantage in the international market.
 Roadmap to transitioning to ODM and proactive global expansion strategy.
 To address the challenge of concentrated risk mitigation and enhance added value, the shift from the OEM (Original Design Manufacturer) model to the ODM (Original Design Manufacturer) model is considered a vital path to survival for Vietnam's wood industry. According to Mr. Ngo Si Hoai, the wood industry needs to enter a new competitive landscape, relying on legally sourced wood, sustainable forest certifications, and design capabilities as its main pillars. Businesses cannot rely on cheap labor or low-quality raw materials; instead, they must invest heavily in modern technology and apply artificial intelligence in production management and design. Developing furniture collections that reflect Vietnamese cultural identity while meeting modern aesthetic standards will help improve the industry's position and maintain higher profit margins.
 Agreeing with this direction, Mr. Le Hoang Tai suggested that state management agencies, the system of Vietnamese trade offices abroad, and industry associations need to coordinate closely to create an ecosystem that supports businesses in effectively transforming. In particular, the Trade Promotion Department will integrate programs to support the enhancement of design capacity and brand building for Vietnamese wood products into the National Trade Promotion Plan. Furthermore, proactive market research by the trade office system will help businesses keep abreast of consumer trends, technical standards, and distribution channels in each export destination.
 In addition, Mr. Ngo Si Hoai proposed building a digital dossier for Vietnam's wood industry and establishing a stable annual trade promotion schedule linked to international and domestic specialized trade fairs and exhibitions.
 Proactively inviting delegations of buyers, retailers, and major distributors from around the world to Vietnam for direct factory surveys will be the most effective on-site promotion channel. The collaboration between VFOREST and local associations such as HAWA, BIFA, and DOWA will create a strong supply chain from raw materials and processing to export trade, helping Vietnamese wood products break free from the shadow of mere processing and confidently assert the "Made in Vietnam" brand on the global trade map.

AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Draft report; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is issuing for public comment a draft report entitled, NUREG-1307, Revision 21, “Report on Waste Burial Charges: Changes in Decommissioning Waste Disposal Costs at Low-Level Waste Burial Facilities.” This report, which is revised periodically, explains the formula acceptable to the NRC for determining the minimum decommissioning fund requirements for nuclear power reactor licensees, as required by NRC regulations. Specifically, this report provides the adjustment factor and updates the values for the labor, energy, and waste burial escalation factors of the minimum formula.
DATES:
Submit comments by November 23, 2026. Comments received after this date will be considered if it is practical to do so, but the Commission is able to ensure consideration only for comments received before this date.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by any of the following methods; however, the NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website:
Federal rulemaking website:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-4588. Address questions about Docket IDs in
Regulations.gov
to Bridget Curran; telephone: 301-415-1003; email:
Bridget.Curran@nrc.gov.
For technical questions, contact the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this document.
Mail comments to:
Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, Mail Stop: TWFN-5-A85, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, ATTN: Guidance and Publications Branch.
For additional direction on obtaining information and submitting comments, see “Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments” in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Emil Tabakov, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001; telephone: 301-415-6814; email:
Emil.Tabakov@nrc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments
A. Obtaining Information
Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-4588 when contacting the NRC about the availability of information for this action. You may obtain publicly available information related to this action by any of the following methods:
NRC's Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS):
You may obtain publicly available documents online in the ADAMS Public Documents collection at
https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams.html.
To begin the search, select “Begin ADAMS Public Search.” For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room (PDR) reference staff at 1-800-397-4209, at 301-415-4737, or by email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov.
Draft NUREG-1307, Revision 21, “Report on Waste Burial Charges: Changes in Decommissioning Waste Disposal Costs
( printed page 66743)
at Low-Level Waste Burial Facilities,” is available in ADAMS under Accession No. ML26271A165.
NRC's PDR:
The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time (ET), Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Submitting Comments
The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website (
https://www.regulations.gov). Please include Docket ID NRC-2026-4588 in your comment submission.
The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at
https://www.regulations.gov
as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. Discussion
Pursuant to section 50.75 of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR), “Reporting and recordkeeping for decommissioning planning,” the NRC requires nuclear power reactor licensees to adjust annually, in current year dollars, their estimate of the cost to decommission their plants. The annual updates are part of the process for providing reasonable assurance that adequate funds for decommissioning will be available when needed.
Revision 21 of NUREG-1307, “Report on Waste Burial Charges: Changes in Decommissioning Waste Disposal Costs at Low-Level Waste Burial Facilities,” modifies the previous revision to this report issued in February 2025 (ADAMS Accession No. ML25037A226) and incorporates updates to the labor, energy, and waste burial escalation factors of the NRC minimum decommissioning fund formula. Due to the inclusion of disposal costs for low activity waste (a subset of low-level waste), unchanged low-level waste (LLW) burial charges at two of the nation's four LLW disposal facilities to which a majority of licensees are anticipated to dispose some portion of their LLW, and slightly to moderately higher charges at the remaining two facilities to which a small number of licensees are anticipated to dispose of their LLW, the minimum decommissioning fund formula amounts calculated by licensees, based on revised LLW burial factors presented in this report, will generally reflect minimum decommissioning fund requirements that are lower, on average, when compared to those previously reported by licensees in 2025.
Acting Chief, Financial Assessment Branch, Division of Decommissioning, Closure, Analysis and Financial Oversight, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards.

Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),[1]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,[2]
notice is hereby given that on October 6, 2026, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act [3]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.[4]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“EDGX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend Rule 19.3 (Criteria for Underlying Securities) and Rule 19.4 (Withdrawal of Approval of Underlying Securities) to (i) establish listing criteria and continued listing standards for options on shares of commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets, (ii) update Rule 19.3(i)(1) to permit the listing of options on an exchange traded fund as defined in Rule 6c-11 under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (“Rule 6c-11”), and (iii) make conforming amendments to remove individual product-specific references and update cross-references within the rules. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 19.3 (Criteria for Underlying Securities) and Rule 19.4 (Withdrawal of Approval of Underlying Securities) to (i) establish listing criteria and continued listing standards for options on shares of commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets, (ii) update Rule 19.3(i)(1) to permit the listing of options on an exchange traded fund as defined in Rule 6c-11 under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (“Rule 6c-11”),[5]
and (iii) make conforming amendments to remove individual product-specific references and update cross-references within the rules.
Background
The Exchange's existing rules permit the listing and trading of options on various types of exchange-traded products, including options on shares of exchange-traded funds (“ETFs”), commodity pool ETFs, currency trust shares, and commodity-based trusts
( printed page 66753)
holding a single crypto asset. Specifically, Rule 19.3(i) sets forth the criteria for securities deemed appropriate for options trading, including Fund Shares that are principally traded on a national securities exchange and defined as an “NMS stock” under Rule 600 of Regulation NMS.
Cboe Options Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe Options”), an affiliate of the Exchange, recently received approval from the Commission to list and trade options on commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets.[6]
Specifically, Cboe Options adopted Rules 4.3.06(a)(6) and 4.4.06(c) to establish initial and continued generic listing criteria for options on commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets.[7]
Additionally, Cboe Options amended Rule 4.3.06(a)(4) to remove individual product-specific references for crypto asset ETPs, and in a separate filing [8]
amended Rule 4.3.06(a)(1) to permit the listing of options on ETFs as defined in Rule 6c-11.
Proposed Rule Changes
The Exchange now proposes to adopt rules that are substantively identical to the Cboe Options Rules described above. Specifically, the Exchange proposes the following amendments.
Amendments to Rule 19.3(i)
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 19.3(i) to establish generic listing criteria for options on commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets. Currently, Rule 19.3(i)(5) permits the listing of options on commodity-based trusts that hold a single crypto asset meeting certain requirements. The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 19.3(i)(5) to also permit the listing of options on commodity-based trusts that hold multiple crypto assets, provided that each underlying crypto asset held by such trust satisfies the following requirements:
i. the total global supply of each underlying crypto asset held by the Commodity-Based Trust has an average daily market value of at least $700 million over the last 12 months; and
ii. each crypto asset held by the Commodity-Based Trust underlies a derivatives contract that trades on a market with which the Exchange has a comprehensive surveillance sharing agreement, whether directly or through common membership in the Intermarket Surveillance Group (“ISG”).
These requirements are designed to ensure that each crypto asset underlying options approved for trading on the Exchange has sufficient market capitalization and is subject to adequate market surveillance. These criteria are substantively identical to those approved by the Commission for Cboe Options.[9]
In addition, the Exchange proposes to update Rule 19.3(i)(1) to permit the listing of options on exchange traded funds as defined in Rule 6c-11, portfolio depositary receipts, or index fund shares. Proposed Rule 19.3(i)(1) is substantively identical to Cboe Rule 4.3.06(a)(1). The requirements of Rule 19.3(i)(1) are generally based on the generic listing standards for exchange-traded funds that pre-dated the adoption of Rule 6c-11.
