articles.title: Elon Musk reportedly invests $1bn in David Ellison’s Skydance
articles.summary: Musk’s investment into the new media empire comes after Paramount’s $111bn merger with Warner Bros DiscoveryElon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk has reportedly invested approximately $1bn in Skydance, the new media empire led by David Ellison.
The deal comes alongside fresh equity infusions from existing investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow. Semafor first reported the news.
The investment follows Paramount’s recent $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, a huge acquisition that brought the media companies together under the Skydance name. At the head of the new media empire is David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison.
The Guardian has contacted Musk and Skydance for comment.
The cash infusion solidifies an alliance between two of Trump’s richest monetary backers. In September, Semafor reported that Paramount executives had considered Musk as an equity investor, citing his close ties to Larry Ellison, who invested $1bn in Musk’s acquisition of X in 2022 and also $45m in support of Trump’s re-election bid in 2024. Musk spent more than $290m on Trump’s re-election bid and has spent more than $350m backing Republicans in the current US midterm elections.
After the merger, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, who previously led Mattel, informed employees that the integration would involve layoffs, stating: “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce.”
The company’s leadership – which now oversees Paramount and Warner Bros’s movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN – has set a target of more than $6bn in cost savings over the next three years, a goal that Los Angeles county officials estimate could lead to the loss of 4,500 film and television jobs in Los Angeles alone.
Prior to the merger, a coalition of 12 states, including California and New York, sued Paramount, arguing that the deal would “extinguish” competition and result in “higher prices, lower quality and less content for film and television”.
In September, a settlement agreement required Skydance to release at least 30 films and more than 180 television shows annually, while ensuring that CBS and CNN maintain editorial independence.

AGENCY:
U.S. Census Bureau, Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice of Information Collection, request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment on the proposed revision to the Annual Business Survey prior to the submission of this information collection request (ICR) to OMB for approval.
DATES:
To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed information collection must be received on or before December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by email to
Matthew.J.Tucker@census.gov.
Please reference Annual Business Survey in the subject line of your comments. You may also submit comments, identified by Docket Number USBC-2026-0562 to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov.
All comments received are part of the public record. No comments will be posted to
http://www.regulations.gov
for public viewing until after the comment period has closed. Comments will generally be posted without change. All Personally Identifiable Information (for example, name and address) voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do not submit Confidential Business Information or otherwise sensitive or protected information. You may submit attachments to electronic comments in Microsoft Word, Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information or specific questions related to collection activities should be directed to Patrice Hall, Assistant Division Chief, R&D and Special Surveys, 301-763-7198,
patrice.n.hall@census.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
In an effort to improve the measurement of business dynamics in the United States, the Census Bureau is conducting the Annual Business Survey (ABS). The ABS combines Census Bureau firm-level collections to reduce respondent burden, increase data quality, reduce operational costs, and operate more efficiently. The ABS measures research and development (R&D), innovation, business owner characteristics, and other topics of interest. The ABS is a joint statistical project between the Census Bureau and the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) within the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF).
The 2026 ABS (collected during 2027) will remove the following business owner demographic questions:
Race
Ethnicity
Sex
Place of Birth
U.S. Citizenship, and
Age
Estimates for this data will be produced through use of various administrative data. The Census Bureau, in collaboration with NCSES, plans to research additional administrative and survey data sources to replace the other owner characteristics questions on the survey in future survey cycles. While this research continues, select business owner characteristics questions (
e.g.,
disability, education level) will remain
( printed page 66670)
on the survey. The Business Enterprise Research and Development survey (BERD), which merged with the ABS beginning with reference year 2025, will continue to be included within the ABS.
The ABS will sample 230,000 businesses and nonprofit organizations (222,000 employer business; 8,000 nonprofit organizations). The ABS includes all nonfarm employer businesses filing Internal Revenue Service (IRS) tax forms as individual proprietorships, partnerships, or any other type of corporation, with non-zero receipts or payroll. Also included are nonprofit organizations to measure their research activities. The ABS samples approximately 8,000 nonprofit organizations who are required to complete IRS form 990. The nonprofit sample will yield national estimates of R&D performance within the nonprofit sector. Of note, nonprofit organizations will only see questions relating to research activities and will not be asked any questions relating to owner demographics.
The ABS is designed to incorporate new content, on a rotating basis, each survey year based on topics of relevance. Each year new questions are submitted to the OMB for approval.
The 2026-2028 ABS will collect the following information from employer businesses:
Company information including sales, employees, and business ownership from all employer businesses.
Select business owner characteristics questions (e.g.,
disability, education level) from the principal owner(s) of the business.
Business characteristics from all employer businesses.
Research, development, and related topics from select businesses and nonprofits.
Innovation data and data on critical and emerging technologies from all employer businesses.
Management practices and employee training data from all employer businesses.
Intellectual property protection and technology transfer data from all employer businesses.
Other potential module topics such as cybersecurity and financing.
II. Method of Collection
The ABS utilizes an online survey instrument. Respondents are mailed and emailed letters directing them to create a Census account and access the survey through their account. The online survey automatically skips questions that do not apply and checks for common errors. Detailed question instructions will be embedded in the electronic instrument where appropriate. Responses will be due approximately 30 days from initial mailing.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC, the Commission) has issued an amendment under exigent circumstances to Renewed Facility Operating License (RFOL) No. DPR-20, issued to Palisades Energy, LLC (the licensee), for operation of the Palisades Nuclear Plant (Palisades, PNP). The amendment modifies the PNP Updated Final Safety Analysis Report (UFSAR) Section 9.11, “Fuel Handling and Storage Systems,” and Section 14.19, “Fuel Handling Accident,” on a one-time basis, to facilitate transport of a fuel assembly designated DD41 from the reactor to the spent fuel pool (SFP) utilizing different plant equipment and following a different travel path than is described in the UFSAR.
DATES:
The amendment was issued on October 13, 2026. A request for a hearing or petitions for leave to intervene must be filed by December 21, 2026.

The NRC issued Amendment No. 283 to RFOL No. DPR-20, to Palisades Energy, LLC (the licensee), under exigent circumstances, which revised the license for operation of the Palisades Nuclear Plant (the facility) located in Van Buren County, Michigan. A publicly available version of the license amendment is available in ADAMS under Accession No. ML26282A040. Documents related to this amendment are listed in the safety evaluation enclosed with the amendment. The amendment was effective as of the date of its issuance.
The amendment modifies UFSAR sections 9.11 and 14.19, on a one-time basis, to describe an alternative fuel-handling process for recovery of tilted fuel assembly DD41. Palisades entered Mode 6 (Refueling) and began loading fuel into the reactor vessel on August 30, 2026. During core reload, fuel assembly DD41 was placed into core location H-1 and tilted over after being released by the refueling machine, coming to rest at an approximate 30-degree angle with the lower tie plate in core location H-1 and the upper tie plate, leaning against the core shroud on the opposite side of the core. Federal Register

The NRC has determined for this amendment that the application for the amendment complies with the standards and requirements of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (the Act), as amended, and the NRC's rules and regulations. Code of Federal Regulations

Title:
Requirements for Recognition as a VA Accredited Organization.
Type of Review:
Revision of a currently approved collection.
Abstract:
In order for an organization to provide representation to claimants before VA regarding claims for VA benefits, the organization must be recognized by VA for that purpose. Section 5902(a) of title 38, United States Code, authorizes VA to recognize organizations for the limited purpose of ensuring competent representation of veterans in claims for benefits administered by VA. VA implemented this authority in 38 CFR 14.628. An organization must apply for VA recognition, supplying information as specified in section 14.628 to demonstrate that it satisfies the legal requirements for recognition. (Organizations may provide services to veterans without VA recognition if the services do not include the preparation, presentation, and prosecution of claims for VA benefits.) The information submitted by the organizations in conjunction with a request for recognition is used by VA in reviewing accreditation applications to determine whether organizations meet the requirements for VA recognition under section 14.628. VA relies on this information to ensure that it is granting recognition only to organizations that can provide long-term, competent representation to VA claimants.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters on the Brownsville Ship Channel. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with an over-sized dead ship tow transiting the area. Entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Corpus Christi, or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective without actual notice from October 22, 2026 through October 24, 2026. For the purposes of enforcement, actual notice will be used from October 20, 2026 until October 22, 2026. The rule will be subject to enforcement on only one day during the effective period when the vessel transits from the sea buoy to the International Shipbreaking Limited dock.
If you have questions about this rule, call or email Lieutenant Commander Timothy Cardenas, Sector Corpus Christi Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 800-874-2143, email
Timothy.J.Cardenas@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received notification that International Shipbreaking will be conducting a dead ship towing operation within the Brownsville Ship Channel near Brownsville, TX. This operation will involve the transit of the decommissioned former United States naval vessel USS VICKSBURG from the sea buoy to the International Shipbreaking Limited Dock. Hazards from this operation include but are not limited to obstruction of vessel traffic, navigational limitations, and various other activities which create potential hazards for workers and the public. The Captain of the Port (COTP) Corpus Christi has determined that potential hazards associated with dead ship towing operations are a safety concern for anyone within the work area. Therefore, the COTP is issuing this rule under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard was notified of this event on October 6, 2026, but we must establish this safety zone by October 20, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain General Electric Company (GE) Model CF34-8C1, CF34-8C5, CF34-8C5A1, CF34-8C5A2, CF34-8C5B1, CF34-8E2, CF34-8E2A1, CF34-8E5, CF34-8E5A1, CF34-8E5A2, CF34-8E5A2HA, CF34-8E6, and CF34-8E6A1 engines. This AD was prompted by reports of in-flight “Engine Degraded” messages from the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) due to corrosion of the variable geometry (VG) system actuator. This AD requires removing certain electronic engine control (EEC) full authority digital electronic control (FADEC) software versions from service and installing an updated EEC FADEC software that is eligible for installation. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-3998; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Daiyun Fang, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th Street, Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: (206) 910-0063; email:
daiyun.fang@faa.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend 14 CFR part 39 by adding an AD that would apply to certain GE Model CF34-8C1, CF34-8C5, CF34-8C5A1, CF34-8C5A2, CF34-8C5B1, CF34-8E2, CF34-8E2A1, CF34-8E5, CF34-8E5A1, CF34-8E5A2, CF34-8E5A2HA, CF34-8E6, and CF34-8E6A1 engines. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on November 18, 2025 (90 FR 51590). The NPRM was prompted by three separate events involving airplanes with Model GE CF34-8C5 engines installed in which “Engine Degraded” messages were received from the EICAS during flight. A subsequent investigation by the manufacturer revealed that these engines had been operated infrequently over the two-year period prior to these events and stored in close proximity to a saltwater coastline. The investigation further revealed the VG actuation lever arms were stuck due to corrosion between the high-pressure compressor case and vane bushings, which increased the VG actuation loads and slowed the VG response. As a result of this increase, the VG command and actual positions exceeded acceptable disagreement parameters, triggering an EICAS “Engine Degraded” message. In response to the “Engine Degraded” message, the manufacturer and FAA determined that certain versions of the EEC FADEC software installed on GE Model CF34-8E and CF34-8C engines can potentially reduce the engine to idle and lock the throttle until the engine is shut down and restarted. In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require removal of certain EEC FADEC software versions from service and installation of updated EEC FADEC software that is eligible for installation. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from three commenters. The commenters were the Airline Pilots Association, International (ALPA), the Citizens Rulemaking Alliance, and Horizon Air. The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Support for the NPRM
ALPA expressed support for the NPRM.
Request To Justify Forgoing Notice and Comment or Issue an NPRM
The Citizens Rulemaking Alliance requested that the FAA place a detailed analysis in the AD docket explaining why prior notice and comment were impracticable for each requirement and why the selected compliance times necessitated immediate issuance. Alternatively, the commenter requested that the FAA either convert this action to an interim final rule limited to actions necessary to mitigate any immediate risk and simultaneously issue an NPRM to solicit comment for 30 to 60 days on non-emergency actions. The commenter asserted the FAA has not adequately justified use of the good cause exception to bypass notice and comment and the 30-day delayed
( printed page 66632)
effective date and must, at a minimum, provide an explanation why a brief comment period was impracticable.
The FAA notes the comment was submitted in response to an NPRM for which the FAA provided a 45-day comment period. This final rule is effective 35 days after its publication in the
Federal Register
. Therefore, the FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Comply With the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
The Citizens Rulemaking Alliance requested that the FAA clarify whether the proposed AD requires reporting. If reporting is required, the commenter requested that the FAA revise the proposed AD to comply with the PRA or suspend the reporting requirement until PRA requirements are satisfied.
The FAA notes that this AD does not require reporting. If an AD were to require reporting, the preamble of the AD would include a paragraph titled “Paperwork Reduction Act” that would provide the applicable OMB control number, required PRA statements, and the estimated time to collect the required information (burden). Any costs associated with the reporting requirement would be included in the Costs of Compliance section in the preamble of the AD. Therefore, the FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Make Incorporation by Reference (IBR) Materials Reasonably Available
The Citizens Rulemaking Alliance stated that the FAA's current practices for IBR frequently fail to meet the legal and regulatory standards for reasonable availability. The commenter called on the FAA to guarantee that all IBR materials are easily and freely accessible to the public and affected parties for both commenting and compliance purposes. The commenter requested that the IBR materials be identified in the proposed AD along with a detailed summary and a statement confirming the reasonable availability of the materials. AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action establishes Class E airspace at Mason District Hospital Heliport, Havana, IL. This action supports new instrument procedures and instrument flight rule (IFR) operations.
DATES:
Effective 0901 UTC, February 18, 2027. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), all comments received, this final rule, and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov.
FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at
www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/.
You may also contact the Airspace Regulation Group, Policy Directorate, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Raul Garza Jr., Federal Aviation Administration, Operations Support Group, Central Service Center, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177; telephone (817) 222-5874.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Mason District Hospital Heliport, Havana, IL, to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9372 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 51405; August 10, 2026) proposing to establish Class E airspace at Mason District Hospital Heliport, Havana, IL. The FAA subsequently published a correction to the NPRM with an extension of the comment period in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 52271; August 13, 2026) to correct a docket number used in two instances. Interested parties were
( printed page 66637)
invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. Two comments were received. One comment expressed support for the NPRM correction.
The other comment criticized the proposed amendment on the grounds that drone operations would be impacted by the proposed airspace dimensions.
In response to this comment, the FAA clarifies that the proposed Class E5 airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface is intended for new IFR procedures to be used by medevac helicopters during poor weather conditions. Accordingly, the FAA has determined that drone operations would not be negatively impacted by this action.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies 14 CFR part 71 by establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 6.4-mile radius of Mason District Hospital Heliport, Havana, IL. This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this heliport to support IFR operations.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action revokes Class E airspace at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. This action supports the instrument procedures being cancelled and the decommissioning of the Santa Elena radio beacon (RBN).
DATES:
Effective 0901 UTC, February 18, 2027. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), all comments received, this final rule, and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov.
FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at
www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/.
You may also contact the
( printed page 66638)
Airspace Regulation Group, Policy Directorate, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Raul Garza Jr., Federal Aviation Administration, Operations Support Group, Central Service Center, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177; telephone (817) 222-5874.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it removes Class E airspace at the affected airport because it is no longer needed to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9901 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 53203; August 17, 2026) proposing to remove Class E airspace at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies 14 CFR part 71 by removing the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. This action is the result of instrument procedures being cancelled and the decommissioning of the Santa Elena RBN.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5(a), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review rulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points (see 14 CFR part 71, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; and Reporting Points); and paragraph B-2.5(k), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review the publication of existing air traffic control procedures that do not essentially change existing tracks, create new tracks, change altitude, or change concentration of aircraft on these tracks. The FAA also determined that no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.
2. The incorporation by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 of FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026, is amended as follows:
Paragraph 6005 Class E Airspace Areas Extending Upward From 700 Feet or More Above the Surface of the Earth.

articles.title: How Long Do Wealth Shocks Persist? Less Than Three Generations in England, 1700–2026
articles.summary:
What happens across generations to wealth shocks? Do they endure and even magnify, or do they dissipate? By implication, how much modern wealth is attributable to events before 1900? This paper uses random shocks to family size in England before 1880 that created wealth shocks for the children to measure the persistence of wealth shocks. […]
The post How Long Do Wealth Shocks Persist? Less Than Three Generations in England, 1700–2026 appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
What happens across generations to wealth shocks? Do they endure and even magnify, or do they dissipate? By implication, how much modern wealth is attributable to events before 1900? This paper uses random shocks to family size in England before 1880 that created wealth shocks for the children to measure the persistence of wealth shocks. Fertility in England before 1880 was a biological lottery. For richer families, family size strongly influenced child wealth. This paper finds that such biology-induced wealth shocks had no impact on descendant wealth by three generations later. Since wealth itself persisted across more than five generations this implies that, in the long run, wealth mainly derives from sources other than inherited wealth. The observed link between nineteenth century and modern wealth does not lie in wealth transfers alone. Wealth persisted because of the familial inheritance of behaviors associated with wealth accumulation and retention.
That is from a recent paper by Gregory Clark and Neil Cummins.  Via the excellent Kevin Lewis.

articles.title: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
articles.summary: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth taxMeta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires.
The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located.
Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years.
Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state.
Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.
In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company.
Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs.
“Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week.
“In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.”
Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings.
The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks.
In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn following a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances
articles.summary: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profitsBarclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.
The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.
The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”
When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.
“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”.
 
She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach.”
The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs in the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.
Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.
It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.
The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expected increase in bank taxes in the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.
When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them.
“I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth.
“This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.”
Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.
It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.
The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.
The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”
Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.
He told the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”

articles.title: French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil
articles.summary: France’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protestsFrench borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 y...
articles.full_text:
French borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.
France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years.
The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002.
The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013.
The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend.
Tens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.
Public buildings were attacked, and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.
Meanwhile, a parliamentary gridlock has blocked plans by the president, Emmanuel Macron, to increase the state pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to rein in state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP.
It comes as the country also grapples with higher inflation triggered by the war in Iran, with many governments with big debt piles coming under acute pressure.
Jim Reid, a market strategist at Deutsche Bank, said the sell-off in French government bonds was starting to ripple out to other countries, too.
“Among others, the Italian 10-year spread over [German bonds] widened 3.8 basis points to 116 basis points, while Spain’s widened 3.1 basis points to 66 basis points, marking its widest level since June 2025,” he said.
Carsten Brzeski of the bank ING said rising yields had reinforced the European Central Bank’s “restrictive” monetary policy stance before its interest rate decision next week. The bank last raised its key interest rate to 2.5% in September.
“The ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December,” he said.
“Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely.”

articles.title: A simple point about the intertemporal regulation of AI
articles.summary:
At some point AI will be more regulated than it is today.  Furthermore, I believe that most parts of the American economy, once they are regulated, end up overregulated. Thus it is likely that the AI sector will, at some point, end up overregulated. Given that reality, perhaps the AI sector should be underregulated today.  […]
The post A simple point about the intertemporal regulation of AI appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
At some point AI will be more regulated than it is today.  Furthermore, I believe that most parts of the American economy, once they are regulated, end up overregulated.
Thus it is likely that the AI sector will, at some point, end up overregulated.
Given that reality, perhaps the AI sector should be underregulated today.  After all, overregulation will have decades, maybe centuries, to catch up and even the ledger.
Many regulatory issues can be considered within this framework.  You can think that AI is “underregulated today”, in the static sense of that term, and still not favor additional regulation right now.  You might prefer to keep it underregulated for some while to come.

articles.title: Do mass shootings in universities lead to permanent effects?
articles.summary:
Using a stacked difference-in-differences design covering shootings between 1990 and 2025, I compare cohorts at affected universities before and after the shooting with cohorts at matched control universities. I find no detectable effects on time to degree, but undergraduates enrolled at the time of the shooting are 4.2% less likely to pursue further studies. Those […]
The post Do mass shootings in universities lead to permanent effects? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Using a stacked difference-in-differences design covering shootings between 1990 and 2025, I compare cohorts at affected universities before and after the shooting with cohorts at matched control universities. I find no detectable effects on time to degree, but undergraduates enrolled at the time of the shooting are 4.2% less likely to pursue further studies. Those who do continue shift toward health: the share of exposed cohorts who later enroll in a health degree rises by 1.3 percentage points (8.8%), and this effect persists among cohorts who enroll after the shooting. Effects on students present during the shooting are consistent with a response to trauma; for later cohorts, I find evidence of sorting, as master’s students with prior healthcare experience become more likely to enroll in affected universities. These results suggest that mass shootings leave institutional and cultural legacies that outlast the students who witnessed them.
That is from the job market paper of María Medellín-Esguerra, who is currently on the job market from Brown University.

articles.title: Cape Cod National Seashore Advisory Commission; Notice of Public Meeting
articles.summary: In accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act of 1972, as amended, the National Park Service (NPS) is hereby giving notice of the 318th meeting of the Cape Cod National Seashore Advisory Commission (Commission).
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
                    SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act of 1972, as amended, the National Park Service (NPS) is hereby giving notice of the 318th meeting of the Cape Cod National Seashore Advisory Commission (Commission).
                    DATES:
The Commission will meet via teleconference and in person on Monday, November 2, 2026. The meeting will begin at 1:00 p.m. and will end by 4:30 p.m. (Eastern).
                    ADDRESSES:
                        The meeting will be held in the classroom at the Salt Pond Visitors Center, 50 Nauset Road, Eastham, Massachusetts 02642. The meeting is open to the public and a virtual participation option will be available for those who are unable to attend in person. Information on joining the teleconference will be available to the public on the Cape Cod National Seashore website at least two weeks prior to the meeting at 
                        https://www.nps.gov/caco/learn/management/advisory-commission.htm.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission was established by section 8 of Public Law 87-126, as amended, and expired on September 26, 2018. The Commission was reestablished by Div. DD, title VI, subtitle B, section 613 of Public Law 117-328, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023. The Commission's new termination date is September 26, 2029. The purpose of the Commission is to consult with the Secretary of the Interior, or his designee, with respect to matters relating to the development of Cape Cod National Seashore, and with respect to carrying out the provisions of the Act establishing the Seashore.
                    Interested persons may make oral presentations to the Commission. Such requests should be made to the Superintendent at the beginning of the meeting. Depending on the number of persons wishing to speak, and the time available, the time for individual comments may be limited. Written comments can be sent to Jennifer Flynn (see 
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                    ). All comments received will be provided to the Commission.
                
The Commission meeting location may change based on inclement weather or exceptional circumstances. If the meeting location is changed, the Superintendent will issue a press release and use local newspapers to announce the change. Detailed minutes of the meeting will be available for public inspection within 90 days of the meeting.
                    Purpose of the Meeting:
                     The Commission will discuss the following:
                
1. Adoption of Agenda
2. Approval of Meeting Minutes from last meeting
3. Superintendent Update: Development Updates
- Planned 2026 construction activities
- Update on the Cable Road (Eastham) Multimodal Trail design and construction project
- Coastal Bluff erosion and park infrastructure: Adaptive Retreat planning
- Park projects being developed and planned for 2027 and beyond
4. Discussion on Cape Cod Character to identify defining natural, landscape and historic features to be preserved within the Seashore boundaries. Cape Cod Character is identified in the Act to establish the Seashore but not defined. Commission members will report out on what their community is protecting through local and regional policy and regulation.
Make recommendations to the Superintendent on characteristics to protect.
5. New Business: Member opportunity to identify emerging issues or future meeting agenda items.
6. Public Comment
7. Adjournment
                    Meeting Accessibility/Special Accommodations:
                     The meeting is open to the public. Please make requests in advance for sign language interpreter services, assistive listening devices, or other reasonable accommodations. We ask that you contact the person listed in the 
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                     section of this notice at least seven (7) business days prior to the meeting to give the Department of the Interior sufficient time to process your request. All reasonable accommodation requests are managed on a case-by-case basis.
                
                    Public Disclosure of Information:
                     Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including your personal identifying information—may be made publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.
                
(Authority: 5 U.S.C. Ch.10.)
                    Alma Ripps,
Chief, Office of Policy.

articles.title: Marine Mammals; File No. 29925
articles.summary: Notice is hereby given that Craig O'Connell, Ph.D., O'Seas Conservation Foundation, Inc., 26 South Shore Drive, Ridgefield, CT 06877, has applied in due form for a permit to conduct commercial and educational photography on cetaceans.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Notice; receipt of application.
                    SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that Craig O'Connell, Ph.D., O'Seas Conservation Foundation, Inc., 26 South Shore Drive, Ridgefield, CT 06877, has applied in due form for a permit to conduct commercial and educational photography on cetaceans.
                    DATES:
Written comments must be received on or before November 23, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        The application and related documents are available for review upon written request via email to 
                        NMFS.Pr1Comments@noaa.gov.
                    
                        Written comments on this application should be submitted via email to 
                        NMFS.Pr1Comments@noaa.gov. Please include File No. 29925 in the subject line of the email comment.
                    
                        Those individuals requesting a public hearing should submit a written request via email to 
                        NMFS.Pr1Comments@noaa.gov. The request should set forth the specific reasons why a hearing on this application would be appropriate.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    The subject permit is requested under the authority of the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972, as amended (MMPA; 16 U.S.C. 1361 
                    et seq.) and the regulations governing the taking and importing of marine mammals (50 CFR part 216).
                
                    The applicant requests a 2-year permit to harass and film cetaceans for a documentary film about the ecological relationships between sharks and cetaceans and the anthropogenic threats they face, including opportunistic filming of sharks feeding on marine mammal carcasses. Up to 5 humpback whales (
                    Megaptera novaeangliae), 5 minke whales (
                    Balaenoptera acutorostrata), 100 common dolphin (
                    Delphinus delphis), 100 Atlantic white-sided dolphins (
                    Lagenorhynchus acutus), and 50 bottlenose dolphins (
                    Tursiops truncatus) may be harassed, observed, and filmed annually by vessel, unmanned aircraft system, and underwater divers.
                
                    In compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 
                    et seq.), an initial determination has been made that the activity proposed is categorically excluded from the requirement to prepare an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.
                
                    Concurrent with the publication of this notice in the 
                    Federal Register
                    , NMFS is forwarding copies of the application to the Marine Mammal Commission and its Committee of Scientific Advisors.
                
                    Dated: October 19, 2026.
Larissa Plants,
Deputy Director, Office of Protected Resources, National Marine Fisheries Service.

articles.title: President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST)
articles.summary: This notice announces a virtual/livestreamed meeting of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST). The Federal Advisory Committee Act requires that public notice of this meeting be announced in the Federal Register.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Department of Energy.
                    ACTION:
Notice of open meeting.
                    SUMMARY:
                        This notice announces a virtual/livestreamed meeting of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST). The Federal Advisory Committee Act requires that public notice of this meeting be announced in the 
                        Federal Register
                        .
                    
                    DATES:
Friday, November 6, 2026; 12-1 p.m. EST.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Purpose of the Board:
                     PCAST advises the President on matters involving science, technology, education, and innovation policy. The Committee provides the President with scientific and technical information that is needed to inform public policy relating to the American economy, the American worker, national and homeland security, and other topics. PCAST responds to requests from the President or co-chairs for information, analysis, evaluation, or advice. In addition, PCAST solicits information and ideas from a broad range of stakeholders including the research community; private sector; universities; national laboratories; state, local and Tribal governments; foundations; and non-profit organizations. PCAST also provides advice in response to requests from the Super Intelligence Task Force.
                
                    Tentative Agenda:
                     (agenda topics are subject to change; please contact Kristen Ellis at 
                    pcast@doe.gov
                     for the most current agenda).
                
- Chair Update
- Charges to the Board
- Board Business
- Public Comments
- Closing Remarks
                    Public Participation:
                     The meeting is open to the public and public comment can be given orally or in writing. Fifteen minutes are allocated during the meeting for public comment and those wishing to make oral comment will be given maximum timeframe of two minutes. To register to speak, please contact 
                    pcast@doe.gov
                     not later than seven days in advance of the meeting.
                
                    Written comments received at least two working days prior to the meeting will be provided to the members and included in the meeting minutes. Written comments received within two working days after the meeting will be included in the minutes. For additional information on public comment and to submit written comment, please contact 
                    pcast@doe.gov.
                     The PCAST welcomes the attendance of the public at its meetings and will make every effort to accommodate persons with physical disabilities or special needs. If you require special accommodations due to a disability, please contact 
                    pcast@doe.gov
                     at least seven days in advance of the meeting.
                
                    Meeting conduct:
                     The Designated Federal Officer is empowered to conduct the meeting in a fashion that will facilitate the orderly conduct of business. Questioning of board members or presenters by the public is not permitted.
                
                    Minutes:
                     Minutes will be available at the following website: 
                    https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/.
                    Signing Authority:
                     This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 20, 2026, by David Borak, Committee Management Officer, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the 
                    Federal Register
                    .
                
                    Signed in Washington, DC, on October 20, 2026.
Jennifer Hartzell,
Alternate Federal Register Liaison Officer, U.S. Department of Energy.

AGENCY:
Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, Science, Technology and Innovation Board (STIB), Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Notice of Federal Advisory Committee meeting.
SUMMARY:
The DoD (referred to herein as “the Department of War” or “DoW”) is publishing this notice to announce that the following Federal Advisory Committee meeting of the STIB will take place.
DATES:
Closed to the public Wednesday, November 4, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Eastern time.
ADDRESSES:
The address of the closed meeting is 1400 Defense Pentagon, Washington, DC 20301-1400.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Elizabeth J. Kowalski, Designated Federal Officer (DFO): (703) 571-0082 (Voice), (Email)
osd.pentagon.ousd-r-e.mbx.stib-office@mail.mil.
Mailing address is Science, Technology, and Innovation Board, 4800 Mark Center Dr., Suite 15D08, Alexandria, VA 22311. Website:
https://stib.cto.mil/.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This meeting is being held under the provisions of chapter 10 of title 5 United States Code (U.S.C.) (commonly known as the “Federal Advisory Committee Act” or “FACA”), 5 U.S.C. 552b(c); and 41, Code of Federal Regulations CFR 102-3.140 and 102-3.150.
Purpose of the Meetings:
The STIB's mission is to provide independent advice and recommendations on matters supporting DoW's scientific, technological, and innovative enterprises. The objective of the meeting is to obtain, review, and evaluate classified information related to the STIB's mission. The STIB will meet with DoW Leadership to receive classified remarks regarding current and future objectives of the DoW and will meet for plenary sessions where the STIB members will have classified discussions regarding a potential Digital Solutions study and a potential Difficult Target Defeat study that may be tasked
( printed page 66694)
to the STIB, as well as having a classified discussion regarding other potential topics of study based on the remarks made by leadership during the meeting.
Agenda:
The meeting will begin at 9:00 a.m. on Wednesday, November 4th. Ms. Elizabeth Kowalski, Designated Federal Officer and Dr. Mitch Nikolich, Chair of the STIB, will provide opening remarks and a classified overview of potential topics that are likely to be tasked to the STIB for study. At 9:30 a.m., the Honorable Steve Feinberg, Deputy Secretary of War, will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding current and future objectives of the Department. Next, from 10:30 a.m. to 11 a.m., the Honorable Michael Duffy will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding modernization efforts for acquisition and sustainment. The Board will have a break from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. From 1:00 p.m. to 1:30 p.m., the Honorable Elbridge Colby will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding National Defense strategy and strategic prioritization. From 1:30 p.m. to 2:00 p.m., Mr. David Lorch will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding integrating and transitioning advanced technologies. This will be followed by a 15-minute break. From 2:15 p.m. to 4:15 p.m., the Board will meet in plenary session to hold a classified discussion regarding study topics currently under consideration by leadership to task the board and to discuss potential studies based on the remarks made by leadership during the meeting. At 4:15 p.m., Dr. Mitch Nikolich will provide closing remarks. The meeting will adjourn at 4:30 p.m.
Meeting Accessibility:
In accordance with section 5 U.S.C. 1009(d) and 41 CFR 102-3.155, the DoW has determined that this STIB meeting will be closed to the public. Specifically, the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, in consultation with the DoW Office of General Counsel, has determined in writing that the meeting will be closed to the public because it will consider matters covered by 5 U.S.C. 552b(c)(1). The determination is based on the consideration it is expected that discussions throughout will involve classified matters of national security concern. Such classified material is so intertwined with the unclassified material that it cannot reasonably be segregated into separate discussions without defeating the effectiveness and meaning of the overall meetings. To permit the meeting to be open to the public would preclude discussion of such matters and would greatly diminish the ultimate utility of the STIB's findings and recommendations to the Secretary of War and to the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
Written Statements:
In accordance with 5 U.S.C. 1009(a)(3) and 41 CFR 102-3.140, interested persons may submit a written statement for consideration by the STIB at any time. Individuals submitting a written statement should submit their statement to the STIB DFO at the email address provided above in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. If a written statement for consideration at a meeting is not received at least three calendar days prior to the meeting, which is the subject of this notice, then it may not be provided to, or considered by, the STIB until a later date. Please note that all submitted comments and statements will be treated as public documents and will be made available for public inspection.
Dated: October 20, 2026.
Stephanie J. Bost,
Alternate OSD Federal Register Liaison Officer, Department of Defense.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is planning to submit an information collection request (ICR), The National Oil and Hazardous Substances Pollution Contingency Plan Regulation, Subpart J (Renewal) (EPA ICR Number 1664.15, OMB Control Number 2050-0141) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act. Before doing so, EPA is soliciting public comments on specific aspects of the proposed information collection as described below. This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through May 31, 2027. This notice allows for 60 days for public comments.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, referencing Docket ID Number EPA HQ-OPA-2207-0042, to EPA online using
www.regulations.gov
(our preferred method), by email to
regulations.gov
(our preferred method), or by mail to: EPA Docket Center, Environmental Protection Agency, Mail Code 28221T, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. EPA's policy is that all comments received will be included in the public docket without change including any personal information provided, unless the comment includes profanity, threats, information claimed to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Rebecca Broussard, Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, Mail Code 5104A, Environmental Protection Agency, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460; telephone numbe: (202) 565-6706; email address:
broussard.rebecca@epa.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through May 31, 2027. An agency may not conduct or sponsor and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
This notice allows 60 days for public comments. Supporting documents, which explain in detail the information that the EPA will be collecting, are available in the public docket for this ICR. The docket can be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
or in person at the EPA Docket Center, WJC West, Room 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The telephone number for the Docket Center is 202-566-1744. For additional information about EPA's public docket, visit
http://www.epa.gov/dockets.
Pursuant to section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, EPA is soliciting comments and information to enable it to: (i) evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (ii) evaluate the accuracy of the Agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (iii) enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (iv) minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate forms of information technology. EPA will consider the comments received and amend the ICR as appropriate. The final ICR package will then be submitted to OMB for review and approval. At that time, EPA will issue another
Federal Register
notice to announce the submission of the ICR to OMB and the opportunity to submit additional comments to OMB.
Abstract:
This Information Collection Request (ICR) renewal supports activities to implement the National Oil and Hazardous Substances Pollution Contingency Plan (NCP), Subpart J (40 CFR 300.900),
Use of Dispersants and Other Chemicals and Biological Agents. The use of bioremediation agents, dispersants, surface washing agents, solidifiers, herding agents and other substances (
e.g.
sorbents) in response to oil spills in U.S. waters or adjoining shorelines is governed by Subpart J of the NCP regulation (40 CFR 300.900). Subpart J requirements include criteria for listing oil spill mitigating agents on the NCP Product Schedule and sorbent products on the Sorbent Product List. EPA's regulation, which is codified at 40 CFR 300.900, requires that EPA prepare a schedule of “dispersants,
( printed page 66700)
other chemicals, and other spill mitigating devices and substances, if any, that may be used in carrying out the NCP.” Requirements under Subpart J of the NCP are required by section 311(d)(2)(G) of the Clean Water Act (CWA), as amended by the Oil Pollution Act of 1990. The NCP Product Schedule and Sorbent Product List are used by Federal On-Scene Coordinators (FOSCs), Regional Response Teams (RRTs), and Area Planners to identify spill mitigating agents in preparation for and response to oil spills. Under Subpart J, manufacturers who want to add a product to the NCP Product Schedule or Sorbent Product List must submit technical product data including applicable toxicity and efficacy testing data to the EPA as stipulated in 40 CFR 300.915. Subpart J requires the manufacturer to submit the corresponding technical product data along with other detailed information to the EPA Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, Office of Land and Emergency Management. The NCP Product Schedule and Sorbent Product List are available to Federal On-Scene Coordinators (FOSCs), Regional Response Teams (RRTs), and Area Committees for helping them select the most appropriate products to use in various spill scenarios.
In June 2023 EPA promulgated a final rule (88 FR 38280, June 12, 2023). This rule revised Subpart J of the NCP by adding new testing and listing criteria for products to be listed on the NCP Product Schedule and establishing the Sorbent Product List. Effective June 10, 2026, only products that are submitted and listed based on the amended testing and listing criteria will be listed on the NCP Product Schedule. All products identified as sorbents prior to the June 2023 rule remained available for use until December 12, 2025, at which time all sorbent products must have submitted information as applicable under the amended testing and listing

articles.full_text: In accordance with the Clean Air Act, as amended (CAA or the Act), notice is given of a proposed consent decree in Our Children's Earth Foundation v. Zeldin, No. 3:25-cv-08994-WHO. On October 19, 2025, Plaintiff Our Children's Earth Foundation filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, San Francisco Division. Plaintiff alleged that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) failed to perform certain non- discretionary duties in accordance with the Act to timely respond to numerous state implementation plan (SIP) submissions from the State of California. AGENCY:
Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) proposes this information collection request (ICR) to revise Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number 1010-0106.
DATES:
Comments must be received by the OMB desk officer no later than November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your written comments on this ICR to the OMB's desk officer for the Department of the Interior at
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
From the
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain
landing page, find this information collection by selecting “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function. Please provide a copy of your comments by parcel delivery service or U.S. mail to the BOEM Information Collection Clearance Officer, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, 45600 Woodland Road, Sterling, VA 20166 or by email to
regulatory.affairs@boem.gov.
Please reference OMB Control Number 1010-0106 in the subject line of your comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Karen Thundiyil by email at
regulatoryaffairs@boem.gov,
or by telephone at 202-742-0970. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside of the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, BOEM provides the general public and other Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on new, proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps BOEM assess the impact of its information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. It also helps the public understand BOEM's information collection requirements and provide the requested data in the desired format.
BOEM published a
Federal Register
notice with a 60-day public comment period on the proposed ICR on May 15, 2026 (91 FR 27981). Five sets of comments were received: three from oil and gas industry stakeholders, one from insurance associations, and one from the general public. Stakeholders broadly support BOEM's proposed revisions, emphasizing improved clarity, reduced ambiguity, and the necessity for restoring stability in the OSFR insurance market. Commenters agree that clarifying coverage triggers aligns with the Oil Pollution Act of 1990. The revised forms are expected to increase insurer participation, expand coverage, reduce premiums, and decrease administrative disputes. Commenters support BOEM's burden hour estimates and recommend electronic submission for efficiency. No comments alter the purpose, need, cost, or hour burden of the ICR.
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burdens, BOEM is again soliciting comments on the proposed ICR. BOEM is especially interested in public comments addressing the following issues:
(1) Is the collection necessary to the proper functions of BOEM?
(2) What can BOEM do to ensure that this information is processed and used in a timely manner?
(3) Is the burden estimate accurate?
(4) How might BOEM enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected?
(5) How might BOEM minimize the burden of this collection on the respondents, including minimizing the burden through the use of information technology?
Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of public record and will be available for public review on
www.reginfo.gov.
BOEM will include or summarize each comment in its ICR to OMB for approval of this information collection.
You should be aware that your entire comment—including your address, phone number, email address, or other
( printed page 66737)
personally identifiable information included in your comment—may be made publicly available at any time. Even if BOEM withholds your personally identifiable information in the context of this ICR, your comment is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 U.S.C. 552). Your information will only be withheld if a determination is made that one of the FOIA exemptions to disclosure applies. Such a determination will be made in accordance with the Department of the Interior's (DOI) FOIA implementing regulations (43 CFR part 2) and applicable law.
For BOEM to consider withholding from disclosure your personally identifiable information, you must identify, in a cover letter, any information contained in the submittal of your comments that, if released, would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of your personal privacy. You must also briefly describe any possible harmful consequences of the disclosure of information, such as embarrassment, injury, or other harm. BOEM will make available for public inspection, in their entirety, all comments submitted by organizations and businesses, or by individuals identifying themselves as representatives of organizations or businesses.
